$comment: Topic list for the IB Biology guide (first assessment 2025). Understanding titles and summaries are paraphrased in our own words; they are not the IB's text. Check against the official guide.

topics.title: Water
big_questions: Which features of the water molecule explain why life depends on it?
How does living in water differ from living in air, and what does that mean for animals?

understandings.title: Water as life's medium
understandings.summary: Know that life began in water and that most biological processes still take place in watery surroundings.

understandings.title: Polar bonds and hydrogen bonding in water
understandings.summary: Explain that oxygen pulls shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, making water polar, so neighbouring molecules attract by hydrogen bonds. Be able to draw at least two water molecules with partial charges and the hydrogen bonds linking them.

understandings.title: Cohesion and why it matters
understandings.summary: Explain how hydrogen bonds make water molecules stick together, allowing water to be pulled up xylem under tension and creating surface tension that lets some organisms live on the water surface.

understandings.title: Adhesion to polar and charged surfaces
understandings.summary: Explain how water is attracted to polar or charged materials and how this drives capillary action through soil and along plant cell walls.

understandings.title: Water as a solvent
understandings.summary: Explain why many hydrophilic substances dissolve in water, making it the medium for enzyme-catalysed metabolism and for transport in plants and animals, while recognising that some cell molecules work precisely because they are hydrophobic and insoluble.

understandings.title: Water versus air for animals
understandings.summary: Compare buoyancy, viscosity, thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity of water and air, and use animals such as the black-throated loon and ringed seal to show the consequences for life in each medium.

understandings.title: Where Earth's water came from and why it stayed
understandings.summary: Describe the hypothesis that asteroids delivered Earth's water, and explain that gravity plus temperatures cool enough for condensation kept it here long enough for life to evolve.

understandings.title: Water and the search for alien life
understandings.summary: Explain why the presence of liquid water guides the search for life elsewhere, including the idea of a Goldilocks zone around a star.

required_skills: Draw two or more water molecules showing partial charges (polarity) and the hydrogen bonds between them

visualisation.reason: Polarity and the hydrogen-bond network only make sense in 3D

topics.title: Nucleic acids
big_questions: How can a chain of just four kinds of building block hold the instructions for a whole organism?
What is it about DNA's shape that lets it be copied so faithfully?

understandings.title: DNA carries genes in all living things
understandings.summary: Know that every living organism uses DNA as its genetic material; some viruses use RNA instead, but viruses are not classed as living.

understandings.title: Parts of a nucleotide
understandings.summary: Identify the phosphate, pentose sugar and nitrogenous base in a nucleotide, drawing them as a circle, pentagon and rectangle in their correct relative positions.

understandings.title: The sugar–phosphate backbone
understandings.summary: Explain how covalent bonds between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next form a continuous, strong backbone in each DNA or RNA strand.

understandings.title: Bases as the letters of the code
understandings.summary: Name the nitrogenous bases found in DNA and RNA and understand that their sequence forms the genetic code.

understandings.title: Building RNA by condensation
understandings.summary: Explain that RNA forms when nucleotides join by condensation reactions, and be able to draw and recognise a single nucleotide and a short RNA polymer.

understandings.title: DNA double helix and base pairing
understandings.summary: Describe DNA as two antiparallel strands held together by hydrogen bonds between A–T and G–C pairs. Draw the strands antiparallel; the helix shape, base sizes and hydrogen-bond counts need not be shown or memorised.

understandings.title: Comparing DNA and RNA
understandings.summary: Compare DNA and RNA by strand number, bases present and pentose sugar, sketch how ribose differs from deoxyribose, and give examples of nucleic acids.

understandings.title: Complementary pairing for copying and expression
understandings.summary: Explain how hydrogen-bond-based complementary base pairing lets genetic information be both replicated and expressed.

understandings.title: DNA's huge information capacity
understandings.summary: Explain that DNA of any length can carry any base sequence, giving an almost unlimited and very compact way of storing information.

understandings.title: Universal code points to common ancestry
understandings.summary: Explain why the near-identical genetic code across all organisms is evidence that life shares one common ancestor; no specific examples need to be memorised.

understandings.title: 5' and 3' directionality
understandings.summary: Describe the 5'-to-3' linkages along nucleic acid backbones and explain why this direction matters for replication, transcription and translation.

understandings.title: Purine–pyrimidine pairs keep the helix uniform
understandings.summary: Explain that each base pair joins a purine to a pyrimidine, so A–T and C–G pairs are equal in length and the helix keeps the same 3D shape whatever the sequence.

understandings.title: Nucleosome structure
understandings.summary: Describe a nucleosome as DNA wound around eight histone proteins, secured by a further histone on the linker DNA, and use molecular visualisation software to explore how the DNA and proteins associate.

understandings.title: Hershey–Chase experiment
understandings.summary: Explain how the Hershey–Chase results, using radioactively labelled phage, showed DNA rather than protein is the genetic material, and note that the experiment depended on radioisotopes becoming available.

understandings.title: Chargaff's base ratio data
understandings.summary: Use Chargaff's data on purine and pyrimidine amounts across species to show how one set of evidence falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis, illustrating falsification as an answer to the problem of induction.

required_skills: Draw nucleotides using circles, pentagons and rectangles for phosphate, sugar and base
Draw and recognise diagrams of a single nucleotide and an RNA polymer
Draw a section of DNA with antiparallel strands and correct A–T and G–C pairing
Sketch the structural difference between ribose and deoxyribose
Use molecular visualisation software to study protein–DNA association in a nucleosome

visualisation.reason: Double helix, antiparallel strands, base pairing and the nucleosome are 3D structures

topics.title: Origins of cells
big_questions: How could non-living chemistry on the young Earth have given rise to the first cells?
What steps might have bridged the gap between simple molecules and a living cell?

understandings.title: Early Earth and pre-biotic carbon chemistry
understandings.summary: Describe early Earth conditions: no free oxygen or ozone, more carbon dioxide and methane, higher temperatures and strong UV. Explain how these may have let carbon compounds form spontaneously in ways that no longer happen.

understandings.title: Cells as the minimum unit of life
understandings.summary: Distinguish living from non-living things and explain why cells are the smallest self-sustaining living units, including why viruses are regarded as non-living.

understandings.title: Why cell origins are hard to explain
understandings.summary: Explain that cells now arise only from existing cells, and that the first cells needed catalysis, self-replicating molecules, self-assembly and compartments. Appreciate that such hypotheses are hard to test because early conditions cannot be recreated and protocells left no fossils.

understandings.title: Miller–Urey experiment
understandings.summary: Evaluate the Miller–Urey experiment as evidence that organic compounds could form from simple inorganic gases under simulated early-Earth conditions.

understandings.title: Self-assembling fatty acid vesicles
understandings.summary: Explain how fatty acids can spontaneously come together into spherical bilayer vesicles, and why an enclosed compartment lets internal chemistry differ from the outside.

understandings.title: RNA as the likely first genetic material
understandings.summary: Explain why RNA, which can both replicate and catalyse reactions, may have served as early cells' genes and enzymes, citing ribozymes in ribosomes that still form peptide bonds.

understandings.title: Evidence for LUCA
understandings.summary: Outline the case for a single common ancestor of all life (LUCA), such as the universal genetic code and genes found in every organism, and why rival early life forms may have died out.

understandings.title: Dating the first cells and LUCA
understandings.summary: Outline approaches used to estimate when the first cells and LUCA existed, and appreciate the vast span of time over which life has evolved.

understandings.title: LUCA and hydrothermal vents
understandings.summary: Describe evidence that LUCA evolved near hydrothermal vents, including fossil traces in ancient vent precipitates and conserved gene sequences found by genome analysis.

required_skills: Evaluate the design and findings of the Miller–Urey experiment

visualisation.reason: Miller–Urey and vesicle self-assembly animate well; much of the topic is conceptual

topics.title: Cell structure
big_questions: What do all cells have in common, and where do different kinds of cell part ways?
How do microscopes let us see and measure the inside of cells?

understandings.title: Cell theory
understandings.summary: Know that all organisms are built from cells, and use this theory deductively to predict that any newly found organism will consist of one or more cells.

understandings.title: Practical microscopy skills
understandings.summary: Gain hands-on experience preparing temporary mounts, staining, focusing with coarse and fine controls, measuring with an eyepiece graticule, calculating magnification and actual size, adding a scale bar and photographing specimens.

understandings.title: Advances in microscopy
understandings.summary: Describe the advantages of electron microscopy, freeze fracture and cryogenic electron microscopy, plus fluorescent stains and immunofluorescence in light microscopy.

understandings.title: Features shared by all cells
understandings.summary: Explain why typical cells all have DNA as genetic material, a mostly watery cytoplasm and a lipid-based plasma membrane enclosing it.

understandings.title: Prokaryotic cell structure
understandings.summary: Describe a Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus or Staphylococcus: cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, a loop of naked DNA and 70S ribosomes. Appreciate that prokaryotes vary, without learning the specific variations.

understandings.title: Eukaryotic cell structure
understandings.summary: Describe the shared eukaryote features: compartmentalised cytoplasm with 80S ribosomes, a double-membraned nucleus with pores and histone-bound chromosomes, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, vesicles and vacuoles including lysosomes, and a cytoskeleton of microtubules and microfilaments.

understandings.title: Life processes in single-celled organisms
understandings.summary: Explain how one cell carries out homeostasis, metabolism, nutrition, movement, excretion, growth, response to stimuli and reproduction.

understandings.title: Animal, fungal and plant cells compared
understandings.summary: Compare these cell types for cell wall presence and composition, vacuole size and role, chloroplasts and other plastids, and centrioles, cilia and flagella.

understandings.title: Atypical eukaryotic cells
understandings.summary: Use nucleus number to show atypical structure in aseptate fungal hyphae, skeletal muscle fibres, red blood cells and phloem sieve tube elements.

understandings.title: Identifying cells and structures in micrographs
understandings.summary: Classify cells in light and electron micrographs as prokaryote, plant or animal, and identify listed structures in electron micrographs, such as nucleoid, nucleus, mitochondrion, chloroplast, sap vacuole, Golgi, rough and smooth ER, ribosomes, cell wall, membrane and microvilli.

understandings.title: Drawing from electron micrographs
understandings.summary: Draw and annotate, with functions, organelles and structures seen in electron micrographs, including nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, sap vacuole, Golgi, rough and smooth ER, chromosomes, cell wall, plasma membrane, secretory vesicles and microvilli.

understandings.title: Endosymbiotic origin of eukaryotes
understandings.summary: Explain that eukaryotes descend from a nucleated, sexually reproducing ancestor that gained mitochondria, and in some lineages later chloroplasts, by endosymbiosis. Cite evidence: 70S ribosomes, naked circular DNA and independent replication in these organelles.

understandings.title: Differentiation into specialised tissues
understandings.summary: Explain that cells in multicellular organisms specialise because they express different sets of genes, often switched on by environmental changes.

understandings.title: How multicellularity evolved
understandings.summary: Know that multicellularity arose many times independently, in many fungi and algae and in all plants and animals, and that it allows larger bodies and specialised cells.

required_skills: Prepare temporary mounts and stain cells and tissues
Focus a light microscope using coarse and fine adjustment
Measure cells with an eyepiece graticule
Calculate magnification and actual size, and add a scale bar
Identify cells as prokaryote, plant or animal in light and electron micrographs
Identify named structures in electron micrographs
Draw and annotate organelles and cell structures from electron micrographs, including their functions

visualisation.reason: Organelles in 3D across cell types; endosymbiosis happens over time

topics.title: Viruses
big_questions: How do viruses manage to reproduce while carrying so little genetic information?
What makes viruses so varied, and how did they come to exist?

understandings.title: What all viruses share
understandings.summary: List the features every virus shares: a small, fixed size; a genome of either DNA or RNA; a protein coat (capsid); no cytoplasm; and very few or no enzymes of its own.

understandings.title: Variety in virus structure
understandings.summary: Describe how viruses differ in shape, in having single- or double-stranded DNA or RNA, and in being enveloped by host membrane or not, using bacteriophage lambda, coronaviruses and HIV as examples.

understandings.title: Lytic cycle
understandings.summary: Describe the stages of the lytic cycle using bacteriophage lambda, and explain that viruses depend on host cells for energy, materials and protein synthesis.

understandings.title: Lysogenic cycle
understandings.summary: Describe the lysogenic cycle using bacteriophage lambda as the example.

understandings.title: Multiple origins of viruses
understandings.summary: Explain why virus diversity points to several separate origins from other organisms, with shared features possibly due to convergent evolution under extreme obligate parasitism, and note that viruses use the same genetic code as living things.

understandings.title: Fast evolution in viruses
understandings.summary: Explain why some viruses evolve very quickly, using influenza and HIV as examples, and discuss what this means for treating the diseases they cause.

visualisation.reason: Lytic and lysogenic cycles are step-by-step processes

topics.title: Diversity of organisms
big_questions: Where should we draw the line between one species and another?
How much do genomes differ within a species compared with between species?

understandings.title: Variation as a hallmark of life
understandings.summary: Every individual differs from every other in some characteristics; these complex patterns of variation are the basis for naming and classifying organisms.

understandings.title: Morphological species concept
understandings.summary: Describe Linnaeus's original idea of a species as a group of organisms sharing similar observable traits.

understandings.title: Binomial naming
understandings.summary: Explain that a scientific name gives the genus first, capitalised, then the species, in lower case, and that species in one genus share similar traits.

understandings.title: Biological species concept
understandings.summary: Define a species as organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring, discuss the problems with this definition, and recognise that other species definitions are in use.

understandings.title: Populations versus species during speciation
understandings.summary: Explain that speciation, one species splitting into several, usually happens gradually as isolated populations diverge, so deciding when they count as separate species can be arbitrary.

understandings.title: Chromosome number varies between species
understandings.summary: Know that chromosome numbers differ widely between species, that humans have 46 and chimpanzees 48, and that diploid cells always carry an even number. No other numbers are required.

understandings.title: Karyotypes and karyograms
understandings.summary: Sort chromosomes in a karyogram by size, banding pattern and centromere position, and evaluate evidence that human chromosome 2 formed by fusion of two ancestral primate chromosomes, as a testable hypothesis.

understandings.title: Genome unity and variation within a species
understandings.summary: Define the genome as an organism's full genetic information, and explain that members of a species share most of it, with differences such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms.

understandings.title: Eukaryote genomes differ in size and sequence
understandings.summary: Explain that eukaryote genomes vary in total DNA content and in base sequence, and that differences between species far exceed those within one.

understandings.title: Comparing genome sizes
understandings.summary: Use a database to find genome sizes for different taxonomic groups and judge whether genome size tracks organism complexity.

understandings.title: Uses of whole genome sequencing
understandings.summary: Describe how sequencing has become faster and cheaper, its current use in studying evolutionary relationships, and its potential future use in personalised medicine.

understandings.title: Species concept fails for asexual organisms and bacteria
understandings.summary: Explain why the biological species concept struggles with organisms that reproduce asexually and with bacteria that swap genes by horizontal gene transfer.

understandings.title: Chromosome number as a species trait
understandings.summary: Explain that members of a species share a chromosome number, and that crosses between related species with different numbers rarely give fertile offspring.

understandings.title: Building a dichotomous key
understandings.summary: Construct a dichotomous key to identify species that live in your local area.

understandings.title: eDNA barcoding to identify species
understandings.summary: Explain how DNA barcodes in environmental DNA samples let scientists quickly identify which species are present and assess a habitat's biodiversity.

required_skills: Classify chromosomes in a karyogram by banding pattern, length and centromere position
Evaluate evidence for the fusion origin of human chromosome 2
Extract genome size data from a database and compare it with organism complexity
Construct a dichotomous key for local plant or animal species

visualisation.reason: Mostly conceptual; karyogram and key tools are enough

topics.title: Classification and cladistics
big_questions: How can we sort millions of species into groups that reflect their real evolutionary history?
What does a cladogram tell us that a traditional ranked hierarchy cannot?

understandings.title: Why classify organisms
understandings.summary: Explain that the huge number of species makes classification necessary and that a good classification opens up many further lines of study.

understandings.title: Problems with ranked taxa
understandings.summary: Explain why the kingdom-to-species hierarchy does not always match evolutionary divergence, why fixed ranks are arbitrary, and how unranked clades in cladistics represent a paradigm shift.

understandings.title: Benefits of evolution-based classification
understandings.summary: Explain that groups whose members all share a common ancestor are ideal, because traits of members can then be predicted from others in the clade.

understandings.title: Clades defined by common ancestry
understandings.summary: Define a clade as an ancestor and its descendants sharing characteristics, and explain that gene or protein sequences give the most objective evidence, though morphology can also be used.

understandings.title: Molecular clock
understandings.summary: Explain how accumulated sequence differences are used to estimate when clades split, and why these are only estimates, since mutation rates depend on generation time, population size, selection pressure and more.

understandings.title: Building cladograms from sequences
understandings.summary: Construct simple cladograms from sample DNA or protein sequence data, using parsimony to choose the tree that needs the fewest sequence changes, and recognise that different criteria can produce different hypotheses.

understandings.title: Reading cladograms
understandings.summary: Use a cladogram to work out relationships, shared ancestors and clades, using the terms root, node and terminal branch; each node represents a hypothetical common ancestor.

understandings.title: Testing classifications with cladistics
understandings.summary: Use a case study, such as the reshuffling of the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae), to show how cladistics revealed groupings based on convergent morphology to be false. Case details need not be memorised.

understandings.title: Three domains from rRNA evidence
understandings.summary: Describe the 1977 reclassification of life into three domains, a level above kingdoms, based on comparing ribosomal RNA base sequences.

required_skills: Construct a simple cladogram from sample base or amino acid sequence data using parsimony
Deduce relationships, common ancestors and clades from a cladogram

visualisation.reason: Reading cladogram topology is easier when you can manipulate the tree

topics.title: Evolution and speciation
big_questions: What lines of evidence convince biologists that species change over time?
How does one species become two, and what keeps them apart afterwards?

understandings.title: Defining evolution
understandings.summary: Define evolution as change in a population's heritable traits, distinguishing it from Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits, and explain why natural selection is called a theory despite overwhelming evidence.

understandings.title: Molecular sequence evidence
understandings.summary: Explain how comparing DNA, RNA and protein sequences provides strong evidence that organisms share common ancestors.

understandings.title: Evidence from selective breeding
understandings.summary: Explain how differences among domesticated breeds and crop varieties, and between them and their wild ancestors, show how quickly evolution can happen.

understandings.title: Homologous structures
understandings.summary: Explain how structures with a shared underlying plan but different uses, such as the pentadactyl limb, support common descent.

understandings.title: Analogous structures and convergent evolution
understandings.summary: Explain that analogous structures do a similar job but evolved separately through convergent evolution, and know at least one example.

understandings.title: Speciation by splitting
understandings.summary: Explain that new species arise only when existing species split, that speciation adds species while extinction removes them, and that gradual change within one lineage is not speciation.

understandings.title: Isolation and differential selection
understandings.summary: Explain how reproductive isolation, for example by geography, and different selection pressures drive speciation, using bonobos and common chimpanzees separated by the Congo River.

understandings.title: Sympatric versus allopatric speciation
understandings.summary: Compare speciation with and without geographic separation, and know that reproductive isolation can be geographic, behavioural or temporal.

understandings.title: Adaptive radiation
understandings.summary: Explain how adaptive radiation lets related species fill vacant niches and coexist without competing, raising ecosystem biodiversity.

understandings.title: Hybridisation barriers and sterile hybrids
understandings.summary: Explain how barriers such as courtship behaviour, and the sterility of hybrids like the mule, stop alleles mixing between species.

understandings.title: Sudden plant speciation via polyploidy
understandings.summary: Explain how hybridisation and polyploidy can create new plant species abruptly, using knotweeds or smartweeds (genus Persicaria) as the example.

visualisation.reason: Speciation happens over time; homologous limbs compare well side by side

topics.title: Conservation of biodiversity
big_questions: Why are species disappearing so quickly today, and how do we know?
Which strategies give threatened species and ecosystems the best chance, and who decides what to save?

understandings.title: What biodiversity means
understandings.summary: Define biodiversity as the variety of life at all levels, covering ecosystem, species and genetic diversity.

understandings.title: Today's species count versus the past
understandings.summary: Explain that many species remain undiscovered, that fossils suggest more species live now than ever before, and that lumpers and splitters may classify the same observations differently.

understandings.title: Human-driven extinctions
understandings.summary: Use at least three case studies of extinctions caused by humans in today's 'sixth mass extinction': the North Island giant moa, the Caribbean monk seal and one extinct species from your own region.

understandings.title: Causes of ecosystem loss
understandings.summary: Examine direct and indirect human causes of ecosystem loss through two case studies: mixed dipterocarp forest in Southeast Asia and, ideally, a lost ecosystem near the student.

understandings.title: Evidence of a biodiversity crisis
understandings.summary: Evaluate evidence such as IPBES reports and repeated surveys of species richness and evenness worldwide, recognising the roles and methodological issues of both professional and citizen scientists and the value of peer review.

understandings.title: Drivers of biodiversity loss
understandings.summary: Explain human population growth as the underlying cause, plus over-exploitation, urbanisation, deforestation and land clearance for farming, pollution, and the global spread of pests, diseases and invasive species.

understandings.title: Multiple conservation approaches
understandings.summary: Explain why no single method suffices, covering in situ conservation and reserve management, rewilding and restoration of degraded land, ex situ conservation in zoos and botanic gardens, and seed or tissue banks.

understandings.title: EDGE species prioritisation
understandings.summary: Explain why the EDGE of Existence programme targets species that are both evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered, and appreciate the ethical, political and economic debate over conservation priorities.

named_examples: a locally extinct species of the student's choice
required_skills: Use data from repeated biodiversity surveys (species richness and evenness) as evidence of change

visualisation.reason: Case studies and data; charts suffice

topics.title: Carbohydrates and lipids
big_questions: Why can small changes in the shape of a sugar or lipid molecule give it a completely different job?
When should an organism store energy as carbohydrate and when as fat?

understandings.title: Why carbon can build so many molecules
understandings.summary: Explain covalent bonding and how carbon forms up to four bonds (single or double) with carbon or other non-metals, giving branched, unbranched and ring-shaped compounds. Know the SI prefixes kilo, centi, milli, micro and nano.

understandings.title: Building polymers by condensation
understandings.summary: Describe how condensation reactions join monomers into polymers, releasing water, using polysaccharides, polypeptides and nucleic acids as examples.

understandings.title: Breaking polymers by hydrolysis
understandings.summary: Explain that hydrolysis splits polymers into monomers by using a water molecule, whose -H and -OH end up on the products.

understandings.title: Monosaccharide structure and glucose's properties
understandings.summary: Recognise pentose and hexose ring structures as monosaccharides. Use glucose to link its solubility, ease of transport, chemical stability and energy yield on oxidation to how cells use it.

understandings.title: Starch and glycogen as energy stores
understandings.summary: Explain why starch (plants) and glycogen (animals) make good stores: coiling and branching make them compact, their size makes them nearly insoluble, and alpha-glucose units are easily added or removed.

understandings.title: Cellulose as a structural polysaccharide
understandings.summary: Relate cellulose's strength to alternating beta-glucose units forming straight chains that bundle together and are cross-linked by hydrogen bonds.

understandings.title: Glycoproteins and cell recognition
understandings.summary: Describe how glycoproteins on cell surfaces allow cells to recognise each other, using the ABO blood group antigens as the example.

understandings.title: Lipids are hydrophobic
understandings.summary: Lipids are a varied group (fats, oils, waxes, steroids) defined by dissolving readily in non-polar solvents but hardly at all in water.

understandings.title: Making triglycerides and phospholipids
understandings.summary: Describe condensation of glycerol with three fatty acids to make a triglyceride, or with two fatty acids plus a phosphate group to make a phospholipid.

understandings.title: Saturated versus unsaturated fatty acids
understandings.summary: Distinguish saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids by number of C=C bonds, link this to melting point, and explain why plants store oils while endotherms store solid fats.

understandings.title: Triglycerides for storage and insulation
understandings.summary: Explain why triglycerides in adipose tissue suit long-term energy storage, and relate their use as heat insulation to an animal's body temperature and habitat.

understandings.title: Why phospholipids form bilayers
understandings.summary: Explain that phospholipids are amphipathic (hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tails) and so spontaneously arrange into bilayers in water. Use the term amphipathic correctly.

understandings.title: Steroids crossing membranes
understandings.summary: Explain that non-polar steroids such as oestradiol and testosterone can diffuse through the bilayer, and identify steroids from their structural diagrams.

required_skills: recognise pentose and hexose monosaccharides from ring-form diagrams
identify steroids from molecular diagrams
use SI prefixes kilo, centi, milli, micro and nano

visualisation.reason: Alpha/beta glucose, cellulose vs starch and fatty-acid kinks are clearer in 3D

topics.title: Proteins
big_questions: How can just twenty building blocks produce proteins with almost any shape or job?
Why does heat or a change in pH stop a protein from working?

understandings.title: General structure of an amino acid
understandings.summary: Draw a generalised amino acid: a central alpha carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable R-group.

understandings.title: Linking amino acids by condensation
understandings.summary: Write the word equation for joining two amino acids and draw a generalised dipeptide, ideally after building it with molecular models.

understandings.title: Essential and non-essential amino acids in diet
understandings.summary: Explain that essential amino acids must come from food while non-essential ones can be made from others; vegans must plan diets to get all essential ones. Named examples are not needed.

understandings.title: Almost unlimited possible polypeptides
understandings.summary: Explain that 20 genetically coded amino acids, in any order and chains of any length from a few to thousands, allow huge variety. Know some example polypeptides.

understandings.title: Denaturation by heat and pH
understandings.summary: Explain how high temperature and pH changes alter a protein's structure, and use the term denaturation.

understandings.title: R-group chemistry drives protein diversity
understandings.summary: Explain that R-groups set a polypeptide's properties: they may be hydrophobic or hydrophilic, and hydrophilic ones may be polar or charged (acidic or basic). Specific R-groups need not be named.

understandings.title: Primary structure determines 3D shape
understandings.summary: Explain that the exact amino acid sequence fixes a protein's three-dimensional conformation, so proteins have precise, repeatable shapes despite their complexity.

understandings.title: Secondary structure: helices and sheets
understandings.summary: Describe how hydrogen bonds at regular intervals along the backbone stabilise alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets.

understandings.title: Bonds that hold tertiary structure
understandings.summary: Explain how hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges between cysteines and hydrophobic interactions stabilise tertiary structure, including how R-group amine and carboxyl groups gain or lose H+ to become charged.

understandings.title: Polar and non-polar amino acids in folding
understandings.summary: Explain that water-soluble globular proteins bury hydrophobic amino acids in their core, while integral membrane proteins have hydrophobic regions that anchor them in the bilayer.

understandings.title: Quaternary structure and conjugated proteins
understandings.summary: Describe proteins made of several chains, contrasting non-conjugated insulin and collagen with conjugated haemoglobin, which has non-protein haem groups. Appreciate how cryo-electron microscopy images single proteins.

understandings.title: Globular versus fibrous proteins
understandings.summary: Contrast the shapes of globular and fibrous proteins and explain how shape suits function, using insulin and collagen as examples.

required_skills: draw a generalised amino acid showing alpha carbon, amine, carboxyl, R-group and hydrogen
write the word equation for dipeptide formation and draw a generalised dipeptide
model condensation of amino acids using molecular models

visualisation.reason: The four levels of protein structure are spatial

topics.title: Membranes and membrane transport
big_questions: How do lipids and proteins self-assemble into a working membrane?
What decides which substances get through a membrane, and how fast?

understandings.title: Lipid bilayers form cell membranes
understandings.summary: Explain that phospholipids and other amphipathic lipids spontaneously form continuous bilayer sheets in water, which is the basis of every cell membrane.

understandings.title: Bilayers as barriers
understandings.summary: Explain that the hydrophobic core of a membrane is poorly permeable to large molecules, ions and polar molecules, so it separates two watery solutions effectively.

understandings.title: Simple diffusion through the bilayer
understandings.summary: Describe simple diffusion across membranes using oxygen and carbon dioxide slipping between phospholipids as the example.

understandings.title: Integral and peripheral proteins
understandings.summary: Distinguish integral proteins (embedded in one or both lipid layers) from peripheral proteins (attached to a surface), and appreciate the variety of membrane protein structures and roles.

understandings.title: Osmosis and aquaporins
understandings.summary: Explain osmosis using random particle motion, membranes that solutes cannot cross and differences in solute concentration, and describe how aquaporins speed water movement.

understandings.title: Channel proteins and facilitated diffusion
understandings.summary: Explain how channel protein structure lets specific ions diffuse through only when the channel is open, making membranes selectively permeable.

understandings.title: Pump proteins and active transport
understandings.summary: Explain that pump proteins use energy from ATP to move specific particles across membranes, which allows movement against a concentration gradient.

understandings.title: How membranes achieve selectivity
understandings.summary: Contrast selective transport by facilitated diffusion and active transport with simple diffusion, which is unselective and depends only on particle size and polarity.

understandings.title: Glycoproteins and glycolipids
understandings.summary: Describe carbohydrate chains attached to membrane proteins and lipids, their position on the outer surface, and their roles in cell adhesion and recognition. Go no further than this.

understandings.title: Fluid mosaic model
understandings.summary: Draw a 2D fluid mosaic model labelling phospholipids, cholesterol, integral and peripheral proteins and glycoproteins, and mark the hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions.

understandings.title: Fatty acid type and membrane fluidity
understandings.summary: Explain that unsaturated fatty acids keep membranes fluid and flexible, while saturated ones strengthen them at high temperature. Know one example of membrane composition adapted to habitat.

understandings.title: Cholesterol as a fluidity buffer
understandings.summary: Describe where cholesterol sits in animal membranes and how it moderates fluidity, stabilising membranes when warm and stopping them stiffening when cold.

understandings.title: Vesicles, endocytosis and exocytosis
understandings.summary: Explain how membrane fluidity allows vesicles to form and fuse, using the terms endocytosis and exocytosis with an example of each.

understandings.title: Gated ion channels in neurons
understandings.summary: Describe neurotransmitter-gated channels, using the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, and voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels.

understandings.title: Sodium–potassium pump
understandings.summary: Describe the sodium–potassium pump as an exchange transporter and explain its importance in setting up membrane potentials.

understandings.title: Sodium-dependent glucose cotransport
understandings.summary: Explain sodium–glucose cotransporters as indirect active transport, and their role in absorbing glucose in the small intestine and reabsorbing it in the nephron.

understandings.title: Cell adhesion molecules and tissues
understandings.summary: Explain that cells stick together into tissues using cell-adhesion molecules (CAMs), with different CAMs for different junction types. Detailed knowledge of specific CAMs or junctions is not needed.

required_skills: draw a 2D fluid mosaic model with phospholipids, cholesterol, integral and peripheral proteins and glycoproteins, marking hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions

visualisation.reason: Fluid mosaic membrane in 3D plus transport processes over time

topics.title: Organelles and compartmentalization
big_questions: Why does dividing a cell into separate compartments make it more efficient?
How does the structure of each organelle fit the job it does?

understandings.title: What counts as an organelle
understandings.summary: Define organelles as discrete cell subunits specialised for a function: nuclei, vesicles, ribosomes and the plasma membrane count; the cell wall, cytoskeleton and cytoplasm do not. Know how ultracentrifuge cell fractionation enabled organelle study.

understandings.title: Benefit of separating nucleus and cytoplasm
understandings.summary: Explain that a nuclear envelope separates transcription from translation, so mRNA can be modified before reaching ribosomes, whereas in prokaryotes ribosomes can meet mRNA straight away.

understandings.title: Compartments in the cytoplasm
understandings.summary: Explain how compartments concentrate enzymes and metabolites and keep incompatible reactions apart, using lysosomes and phagocytic vacuoles as examples.

understandings.title: Mitochondrion adapted for aerobic respiration
understandings.summary: Relate mitochondrial structure to ATP production: a double membrane enclosing a small intermembrane space, folded cristae with large surface area, and a matrix holding Krebs cycle enzymes and substrates.

understandings.title: Chloroplast adapted for photosynthesis
understandings.summary: Relate chloroplast structure to function: extensive thylakoid membranes carrying photosystems, small fluid volumes inside thylakoids, and Calvin cycle enzymes and substrates concentrated in the stroma.

understandings.title: Double membrane of the nucleus
understandings.summary: Explain the benefits of the nuclear double membrane, why it needs pores, and why it breaks into vesicles during mitosis and meiosis.

understandings.title: Free ribosomes and rough ER
understandings.summary: Contrast free ribosomes, which make proteins kept in the cell, with ribosomes on the rough ER, which make proteins for transport elsewhere or secretion.

understandings.title: Golgi apparatus
understandings.summary: Describe the Golgi apparatus structure and its role in processing proteins and preparing them for secretion. Other Golgi functions are not required.

understandings.title: Vesicles and clathrin
understandings.summary: Describe the structure and roles of vesicles in moving materials around the cell, including how clathrin helps vesicles form.

visualisation.reason: Mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus and ER→Golgi→vesicle traffic are 3D and dynamic

topics.title: Cell specialization
big_questions: How does one fertilised egg give rise to hundreds of very different cell types?
Why are cells small, and how do specialised cells get around the limits of size?

understandings.title: From zygote to specialised cells
understandings.summary: Describe how fertilisation produces unspecialised cells that then differentiate, and explain how chemical gradients in the early embryo switch different genes on in different cells.

understandings.title: What makes a stem cell
understandings.summary: State the two defining properties of stem cells: they can keep dividing indefinitely and can differentiate along different pathways.

understandings.title: Stem cell niches in adults
understandings.summary: Describe two locations of adult stem cell niches, such as bone marrow and hair follicles, and explain that a niche can keep stem cells dormant or trigger their division and differentiation.

understandings.title: Totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent
understandings.summary: Distinguish the three levels of potency: early embryo cells are totipotent, soon becoming pluripotent, while adult stem cells such as those in bone marrow are multipotent.

understandings.title: Cell size in specialised human cells
understandings.summary: Compare sizes of human cells including sperm and egg, red and white blood cells, neurons and striated muscle fibres, linking size to specialisation.

understandings.title: Surface area-to-volume ratio limits size
understandings.summary: Explain mathematically why volume grows faster than surface area, so larger cells exchange materials less effectively. Model this with cubes of different side lengths, recognising models simplify reality.

understandings.title: Increasing surface area-to-volume ratio
understandings.summary: Describe how flattening, microvilli and infolding (invagination) raise SA:V, using red blood cells and proximal convoluted tubule cells of the nephron as examples.

understandings.title: Type I and type II pneumocytes
understandings.summary: Explain that very thin type I pneumocytes shorten diffusion distance, while type II pneumocytes release surfactant from lamellar bodies; alveolar lining shows a tissue needing more than one cell type.

understandings.title: Cardiac versus striated muscle cells
understandings.summary: Compare cardiac muscle cells and striated muscle fibres: both contain myofibrils but differ in branching, length and nucleus number. Suggest reasons for the differences and debate whether a muscle fibre is a cell.

understandings.title: Adaptations of human sperm and eggs
understandings.summary: Describe the structural adaptations of human sperm and egg cells to their roles in fertilisation. Only human gametes are required.

named_examples: type I and type II pneumocytes
required_skills: calculate surface area, volume and SA:V for cubes of different side lengths

visualisation.reason: SA:V is a variable relationship; cell adaptations compare well side by side

topics.title: Gas exchange
big_questions: Why do bigger organisms need special organs for gas exchange?
How do a leaf and a lung solve the same problem in different ways?

understandings.title: Why every organism must exchange gases
understandings.summary: Explain that gas exchange gets harder as organisms grow, because SA:V falls and the distance from the centre to the outside increases.

understandings.title: Features of gas-exchange surfaces
understandings.summary: List and explain the properties of good gas-exchange surfaces: permeable, thin, moist and with a large surface area.

understandings.title: Keeping concentration gradients steep
understandings.summary: Explain how dense capillary networks, continuous blood flow and ventilation (air in lungs, water over gills) maintain diffusion gradients in animals.

understandings.title: Mammalian lung adaptations
understandings.summary: Describe how alveolar lungs are adapted, including surfactant, branching bronchioles, extensive capillary beds and very large surface area. Only mammalian lungs are needed.

understandings.title: Breathing in and out
understandings.summary: Explain lung ventilation in terms of the diaphragm, intercostal muscles, abdominal muscles and ribs changing chest volume and pressure.

understandings.title: Measuring lung volumes
understandings.summary: Take measurements to find tidal volume, vital capacity, and inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes.

understandings.title: Leaf adaptations for gas exchange
understandings.summary: Relate leaf structures to gas exchange: waxy cuticle, epidermis, air spaces, spongy mesophyll, guard cells controlling stomata, and veins.

understandings.title: Tissue layout in a leaf
understandings.summary: Draw and label a plan diagram showing where tissues lie in a transverse section of a dicot leaf.

understandings.title: Transpiration as a side effect
understandings.summary: Explain that water loss by transpiration is an unavoidable result of gas exchange through stomata, and know the factors that change its rate.

understandings.title: Measuring stomatal density
understandings.summary: Determine stomatal density from micrographs or leaf casts, repeating counts to show biological variability and improve reliability.

understandings.title: Foetal and adult haemoglobin
understandings.summary: Compare foetal and adult haemoglobin, explaining cooperative oxygen binding to haem groups and allosteric binding of carbon dioxide.

understandings.title: Bohr shift
understandings.summary: Explain how higher carbon dioxide levels make haemoglobin release more oxygen and why this helps actively respiring tissues.

understandings.title: Oxygen dissociation curves
understandings.summary: Interpret oxygen dissociation curves as showing haemoglobin's oxygen affinity at different oxygen levels, and explain the S-shape through cooperative binding.

required_skills: measure tidal volume, vital capacity and inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes
draw and label a plan diagram of a transverse section of a dicot leaf
determine stomatal density from micrographs or leaf casts with repeated counts
interpret oxygen dissociation curves including the Bohr shift

visualisation.reason: Alveolus in 3D, ventilation over time, oxygen dissociation curve and Bohr shift

topics.title: Transport
big_questions: How do animals and plants move fluids around large bodies using pressure?
In what ways are blood vessels and xylem alike, and how are they different?

understandings.title: Capillary adaptations for exchange
understandings.summary: Explain how capillaries suit exchange: branching and narrow diameter give large surface area, walls are thin, and some have fenestrations where very rapid exchange is needed.

understandings.title: Telling arteries from veins
understandings.summary: Identify arteries and veins in micrographs using wall structure and wall thickness relative to lumen diameter.

understandings.title: Arteries carry high-pressure blood
understandings.summary: Explain how muscle and elastic tissue layers in artery walls let them withstand and maintain high blood pressure as blood leaves the heart.

understandings.title: Measuring pulse rate
understandings.summary: Find heart rate by feeling the radial or carotid pulse, and compare this with digital measurement methods.

understandings.title: Veins return blood to the heart
understandings.summary: Explain how valves stop backflow and flexible walls let surrounding muscles squeeze veins, helping low-pressure blood return to the heart.

understandings.title: Coronary artery occlusion
understandings.summary: Explain causes and effects of blocked coronary arteries and evaluate epidemiological data on coronary heart disease, using correlation coefficients while recognising correlation does not prove causation.

understandings.title: Water movement from roots to leaves
understandings.summary: Explain the transpiration pull: evaporation from leaf cell walls draws water out of xylem by capillary action, creating tension, while cohesion keeps the water column unbroken.

understandings.title: Xylem vessel adaptations
understandings.summary: Relate xylem structure to function: no cell contents and missing end walls for free flow, lignified walls to resist tension, and pits for water entry and exit.

understandings.title: Tissues in a dicot stem section
understandings.summary: Draw plan diagrams of a dicot stem cross-section from micrographs showing vascular bundles, xylem, phloem, cortex and epidermis, annotated with their main functions.

understandings.title: Tissues in a dicot root section
understandings.summary: Draw diagrams of a dicot root cross-section from micrographs identifying the vascular tissue, xylem, phloem, cortex and epidermis.

understandings.title: Forming and reabsorbing tissue fluid
understandings.summary: Explain that high arteriole-end pressure forces plasma out of capillaries as tissue fluid, and lower pressure at the venule end lets it drain back in.

understandings.title: Tissue fluid exchange with cells
understandings.summary: Describe how substances pass between tissue fluid and body cells, and compare the composition of plasma with tissue fluid.

understandings.title: Lymph drainage
understandings.summary: Explain how excess tissue fluid enters thin-walled, gapped lymph ducts with valves and is returned to the blood. Go no further than this.

understandings.title: Single versus double circulation
understandings.summary: Compare single circulation in bony fish with double circulation in mammals using simple circuit diagrams showing the order of organs blood passes through.

understandings.title: Heart structure for pumping
understandings.summary: Relate cardiac muscle, pacemaker, atria, ventricles, AV and semilunar valves, septum and coronary vessels to function; label them on a frontal-section heart diagram and trace blood flow from named veins to arteries.

understandings.title: Cardiac cycle
understandings.summary: Describe the sequence of events on the left side of the heart after the sinoatrial node starts a beat, and interpret systolic and diastolic pressures from data and graphs.

understandings.title: Root pressure
understandings.summary: Explain that active transport of mineral ions into roots creates positive root pressure, which moves water up when transpiration is too low, such as in humid conditions or before leaves open in spring.

understandings.title: Phloem sieve tubes and companion cells
understandings.summary: Relate sieve plates, reduced cytoplasm, no nucleus in sieve tube elements, mitochondria-rich companion cells and linking plasmodesmata to easy sap flow and loading at sources and unloading at sinks.

named_examples: saturated fat intake and coronary heart disease correlation
phloem sieve tubes and companion cells
required_skills: distinguish arteries and veins in micrographs
measure heart rate from the carotid or radial pulse and compare with digital methods
evaluate epidemiological data on coronary heart disease using correlation coefficients
draw and annotate plan diagrams of a dicot stem transverse section from micrographs
draw diagrams of a dicot root transverse section from micrographs
draw simple circuit diagrams of single and double circulation
label a frontal-plane heart diagram and trace blood flow from veins to arteries
interpret systolic and diastolic blood pressure data and graphs

visualisation.reason: Heart and cardiac cycle, transpiration and tissue fluid are processes over time

topics.title: Muscle and motility
big_questions: What happens inside a muscle at the molecular level when it shortens?
Why is the ability to move, or to stay put, such an important adaptation?

understandings.title: Movement across living things
understandings.summary: Explore how organisms are adapted for movement by comparing a range of species, including at least one motile and one sessile example.

understandings.title: Sliding filament model
understandings.summary: Explain how a sarcomere shortens as myosin and actin filaments slide past one another.

understandings.title: Titin and antagonistic muscles in relaxation
understandings.summary: Explain that titin helps sarcomeres spring back after stretching and prevents overstretching, and that muscles work in antagonistic pairs because they can only pull when contracting.

understandings.title: Motor units
understandings.summary: Describe a motor unit as a motor neuron, the muscle fibres it controls, and the neuromuscular junctions linking them.

understandings.title: Skeletons as anchors and levers
understandings.summary: Explain how skeletons give muscles attachment points and act as levers, comparing arthropod exoskeletons with vertebrate endoskeletons.

understandings.title: Synovial joint movement
understandings.summary: Using the human hip, describe the roles of bones, cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, muscles and tendons. Name the femur and pelvis; individual muscles and ligaments need not be named.

understandings.title: Measuring range of motion
understandings.summary: Compare how far a joint can move in different planes, measuring joint angles with a goniometer or computer image analysis.

understandings.title: Intercostal muscles as antagonists
understandings.summary: The internal and external intercostal muscles have fibres at different angles, so they pull the ribs in opposite directions; when one layer contracts it stretches the other, storing energy in titin.

understandings.title: Why animals move from place to place
understandings.summary: Describe reasons for locomotion, namely finding food, escaping danger, finding a mate and migrating, giving at least one named example of each.

understandings.title: Swimming adaptations of marine mammals
understandings.summary: Describe how marine mammals are adapted for swimming: streamlined bodies, limbs modified into flippers, a tail fluke moved up and down, and airway changes allowing breathing between dives.

named_examples: one motile and one sessile species
required_skills: measure joint angles using a goniometer or computer analysis of images
compare range of motion of a joint in several dimensions

visualisation.reason: Sliding filaments in a sarcomere happen in 3D over time

topics.title: Adaptation to environment
big_questions: How do the physical conditions of a place shape the organisms that can live there?
Why do distant places with similar climates end up with similar-looking ecosystems?

understandings.title: What a habitat is
understandings.summary: Define habitat as where an organism, population, species or community lives, describable by geographical and physical location and by ecosystem type.

understandings.title: Adaptations to abiotic conditions
understandings.summary: Describe how organisms are adapted to the non-living conditions of their habitat, using a sand-dune grass and a mangrove tree as examples.

understandings.title: Abiotic factors and where species live
understandings.summary: Give examples of abiotic variables that limit where plants and animals are found, and explain that a species' adaptations give it a range of tolerance.

understandings.title: Tolerance ranges from transect data
understandings.summary: Collect your own transect data in a natural or semi-natural habitat, measuring abiotic variables (possibly with sensors), and correlate species distribution with an abiotic factor.

understandings.title: What coral reefs need
understandings.summary: Using coral reefs as a marine ecosystem example, explain how water depth, pH, salinity, clarity and temperature determine where reefs form.

understandings.title: Climate determines biome distribution
understandings.summary: Explain that each combination of temperature and rainfall tends to produce one ecosystem type, shown on a graph with these two variables as axes.

understandings.title: Biomes and convergent evolution
understandings.summary: Explain that biomes are groups of similar ecosystems arising from similar climates and convergent evolution; know the climates of tropical forest, temperate forest, taiga, grassland, tundra and hot desert.

understandings.title: Hot desert and rainforest adaptations
understandings.summary: Describe adaptations of named plant and animal species to life in hot deserts and in tropical rainforests.

named_examples: sand dune grass species (e.g. marram grass)
named hot desert and tropical rainforest plants and animals
required_skills: collect transect data in a natural or semi-natural habitat and correlate species distribution with an abiotic variable
measure abiotic variables such as temperature, light intensity and soil pH, possibly with sensors
interpret a biome graph with temperature and rainfall on the axes

visualisation.reason: Biome and tolerance graphs suffice

topics.title: Ecological niches
big_questions: What are the many different ways organisms get the energy and matter they need?
How do competing species share an ecosystem without one always winning?

understandings.title: The niche as a species' role
understandings.summary: A species' niche is its role in the ecosystem: all the biotic and abiotic interactions that affect its survival, growth and reproduction, including how it gets its food.

understandings.title: Obligate and facultative anaerobes and aerobes
understandings.summary: Distinguish obligate anaerobes, facultative anaerobes and obligate aerobes by whether they tolerate or need oxygen. Only oxygen tolerance is required.

understandings.title: Photosynthetic nutrition
understandings.summary: State that plants, algae and several groups of prokaryotes feed by photosynthesis. Details of prokaryote photosynthesis types are not needed.

understandings.title: Holozoic nutrition in animals
understandings.summary: Explain that all animals are heterotrophs and that holozoic nutrition involves ingesting, digesting internally, absorbing and assimilating food.

understandings.title: Mixotrophic protists
understandings.summary: Explain mixotrophy, combining autotrophic and heterotrophic feeding, using Euglena and oceanic plankton, and distinguish obligate from facultative mixotrophs.

understandings.title: Saprotrophs as decomposers
understandings.summary: Describe saprotrophic nutrition in some fungi and bacteria, which feed on dead matter and act as decomposers.

understandings.title: Varied nutrition in archaea
understandings.summary: Archaea form one of the three domains and obtain energy for ATP production from a remarkably wide range of sources; no named examples are needed.

understandings.title: Hominid teeth and diet
understandings.summary: Infer the diet of herbivorous and omnivorous hominids from skull and teeth features using models or digital collections, for example Homo sapiens, Homo floresiensis and Paranthropus robustus.

understandings.title: Herbivores versus plant defences
understandings.summary: Describe herbivore adaptations such as piercing and chewing insect mouthparts, plant defences such as thorns and toxic secondary compounds, and animal adaptations for detoxifying these toxins.

understandings.title: Predator and prey adaptations
understandings.summary: Describe chemical, physical and behavioural adaptations predators use to find, catch and kill prey, and that prey use to avoid being eaten.

understandings.title: Plant strategies for capturing light
understandings.summary: Using forest examples, describe how canopy trees, lianas, epiphytes, strangler epiphytes and shade-tolerant shrubs and herbs on the forest floor each obtain light.

understandings.title: Fundamental and realized niches
understandings.summary: Distinguish the fundamental niche, set by a species' adaptations and tolerances, from the realized niche it actually occupies when competing with other species.

understandings.title: Competitive exclusion
understandings.summary: Explain that two species cannot share an identical niche: competition either eliminates one species or restricts both to part of their fundamental niches.

required_skills: examine models or digital collections of hominid skulls to infer diet from dentition

visualisation.reason: Niche and competitive exclusion are relationships between variables

topics.title: Enzymes and metabolism
big_questions: How does an enzyme's shape let it speed up one particular reaction?
How do thousands of linked reactions in a cell stay coordinated and under control?

understandings.title: Enzymes speed up cell reactions
understandings.summary: Enzymes are biological catalysts; explain why cells benefit from reactions running much faster than they would without a catalyst.

understandings.title: Enzymes control the metabolic network
understandings.summary: Metabolism is a web of interlinked reactions. Because each enzyme is specific, organisms need many different enzymes, and controlling enzymes is how metabolism is regulated.

understandings.title: Anabolism versus catabolism
understandings.summary: Anabolism builds macromolecules from monomers by condensation (e.g. protein synthesis, glycogen formation, photosynthesis); catabolism breaks them down, e.g. hydrolysis in digestion and oxidation of substrates in respiration.

understandings.title: Globular enzymes and their active sites
understandings.summary: Enzymes are globular proteins. The active site is made of only a few amino acids, but the whole 3D fold of the protein gives it the properties needed for catalysis.

understandings.title: Induced fit between substrate and enzyme
understandings.summary: Describe induced-fit binding, recognising that the shapes of both the substrate and the enzyme change as they bind.

understandings.title: Molecular motion and collisions in catalysis
understandings.summary: Substrate and active site must collide to react, so molecular movement matters; note that sometimes the substrate is fixed in place (large molecules) and sometimes the enzyme is (embedded in membranes).

understandings.title: Active site shape, specificity and denaturation
understandings.summary: Be able to explain how the active site's structure gives an enzyme its specificity for a substrate, and how denaturation alters that structure and stops catalysis.

understandings.title: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration effects
understandings.summary: Explain how temperature, pH and substrate concentration affect enzyme activity using collision theory and denaturation; interpret graphs of these effects and treat sketch graphs as models testable with experimental data.

understandings.title: Measuring enzyme reaction rates
understandings.summary: Work out rates of enzyme-catalysed reactions both from your own experiments and from secondary data.

understandings.title: Enzymes lower activation energy
understandings.summary: Energy is needed to break substrate bonds and released when product bonds form; enzymes reduce the activation energy. Interpret energy diagrams showing this.

understandings.title: Reactions inside versus outside cells
understandings.summary: Contrast intracellular enzyme reactions (glycolysis and the Krebs cycle) with extracellular ones such as chemical digestion in the gut.

understandings.title: Metabolism releases heat
understandings.summary: Because metabolic energy transfers are never fully efficient, heat is always produced; mammals, birds and some other animals rely on this heat to keep body temperature constant.

understandings.title: Linear and cyclical metabolic pathways
understandings.summary: Distinguish linear from cyclical pathways using glycolysis (linear) and the Krebs and Calvin cycles (cyclical) as examples.

understandings.title: Allosteric sites and non-competitive inhibition
understandings.summary: Only specific molecules fit an allosteric site; their reversible binding changes the enzyme's conformation so the active site no longer catalyses the reaction.

understandings.title: Competitive inhibition at the active site
understandings.summary: A competitive inhibitor reversibly occupies the active site (example: statins). Compare competitive and non-competitive inhibition, including how raising substrate concentration affects each.

understandings.title: End-product feedback inhibition
understandings.summary: Explain how an end product inhibits an early enzyme in its own pathway, using isoleucine synthesis as the example.

understandings.title: Irreversible mechanism-based inhibition
understandings.summary: Some inhibitors bind permanently and chemically alter the active site; use penicillin acting on transpeptidases, and explain how altered transpeptidases give bacteria penicillin resistance.

required_skills: interpret graphs of enzyme activity against temperature, pH and substrate concentration
evaluate sketch-graph models using experimental enzyme data
determine reaction rates from experiments and secondary data
interpret activation-energy graphs

visualisation.reason: Rate vs temperature, pH and substrate concentration, and inhibition types, are variable relationships

topics.title: Cell respiration
big_questions: How do cells capture energy from food molecules in a form they can spend?
Why does having oxygen make such a difference to how much ATP a cell can make?

understandings.title: ATP as the cell's energy currency
understandings.summary: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a nucleotide; know its full name and the properties that make it well suited to carrying and distributing energy within cells.

understandings.title: Cell processes powered by ATP
understandings.summary: ATP fuels active transport across membranes, anabolic synthesis of macromolecules, and movement of whole cells or parts of cells such as chromosomes.

understandings.title: Energy changes in ATP–ADP interconversion
understandings.summary: Hydrolysing ATP to ADP and phosphate releases energy, while making ATP from them requires energy. No kilojoule values needed, only that the amount suits many cell tasks.

understandings.title: Respiration makes ATP from carbon compounds
understandings.summary: Cell respiration releases energy from organic compounds (mainly glucose and fatty acids, but many others possible) to make ATP; distinguish respiration from gas exchange.

understandings.title: Aerobic versus anaerobic respiration in humans
understandings.summary: Compare substrates, oxygen need, relative ATP yield, waste products and location in the cell; write word equations for both with glucose, noting only aerobic respiration needs mitochondria.

understandings.title: Factors affecting respiration rate
understandings.summary: Take measurements to find the rate of cell respiration and calculate rates from your own raw data or from secondary data.

understandings.title: NAD as a hydrogen carrier in oxidation
understandings.summary: Oxidation is loss of electrons, so removing hydrogen (dehydrogenation) oxidises a substrate. Redox reactions pair oxidation with reduction; NAD is reduced when it gains hydrogen.

understandings.title: Glycolysis: glucose to pyruvate
understandings.summary: Outline glycolysis as phosphorylation, lysis, oxidation and ATP formation, giving a net gain of ATP and reduced NAD; each step uses a different enzyme, but intermediate names are not needed.

understandings.title: Lactate formation regenerates NAD
understandings.summary: In anaerobic respiration in humans, pyruvate is reduced to lactate. This regenerates NAD so glycolysis can continue, giving only 2 ATP (net) per glucose.

understandings.title: Yeast fermentation in brewing and baking
understandings.summary: Yeast and human anaerobic pathways match except for how pyruvate regenerates NAD, giving different end products; relate yeast's products to brewing and baking.

understandings.title: The link reaction
understandings.summary: Pyruvate is oxidised and decarboxylated to an acetyl group (2C); carbohydrates and lipids both yield acetyl groups, which coenzyme A carries into the Krebs cycle.

understandings.title: The Krebs cycle
understandings.summary: Acetyl joins oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C); the cycle's four oxidations (dehydrogenations) and two decarboxylations regenerate oxaloacetate, producing ATP and reduced NAD. Only citrate and oxaloacetate need naming.

understandings.title: Reduced NAD feeds the electron transport chain
understandings.summary: Reduced NAD made in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle passes a pair of electrons to the first carrier of the electron transport chain and is re-oxidised to NAD.

understandings.title: Electron flow builds a proton gradient
understandings.summary: Explain how electrons passing along the transport chain pump protons to create a gradient; names of the protein complexes are not required.

understandings.title: Chemiosmosis and ATP synthase in mitochondria
understandings.summary: Explain how ATP synthase uses the energy of protons flowing down their gradient to phosphorylate ADP into ATP.

understandings.title: Oxygen as the final electron acceptor
understandings.summary: Oxygen takes electrons from the end of the chain plus protons from the matrix, forming metabolic water and keeping electrons flowing.

understandings.title: Lipids versus carbohydrates as respiratory fuels
understandings.summary: Lipids release more energy per gram (less oxygen, more oxidisable H and C). Only carbohydrate enters glycolysis or anaerobic respiration; fatty acids enter as 2C acetyl groups via acetyl-CoA.

required_skills: write word equations for aerobic and anaerobic respiration of glucose
measure and calculate rates of cell respiration from experimental or secondary data

visualisation.reason: Respiration stages are located in a 3D mitochondrion; chemiosmosis happens over time

topics.title: Photosynthesis
big_questions: How does a leaf turn light into the chemical energy stored in sugar?
What sets the upper limit on how fast a plant can photosynthesise?

understandings.title: Light energy becomes chemical energy
understandings.summary: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy in carbon compounds, and this supplies most of the chemical energy used by life in ecosystems.

understandings.title: Carbon dioxide reduced using hydrogen from water
understandings.summary: Photosynthesis reduces carbon dioxide to glucose using hydrogen obtained by splitting water; be able to give the word equation.

understandings.title: Oxygen released as a by-product
understandings.summary: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria release oxygen as a by-product; know the word equation and that the oxygen comes from splitting water molecules.

understandings.title: Chromatography of photosynthetic pigments
understandings.summary: Separate pigments by thin-layer or paper chromatography, calculate Rf values, and identify each pigment by its colour and Rf value.

understandings.title: Pigments absorb particular wavelengths
understandings.summary: Absorbed light excites electrons in pigment molecules, converting light to chemical energy; explain why only some wavelengths are absorbed and read absorption spectra labelled with both wavelengths and colours.

understandings.title: Absorption spectra compared with action spectra
understandings.summary: Compare absorption and action spectra; calculate photosynthesis rates at different wavelengths from oxygen output or carbon dioxide uptake and plot these as an action spectrum.

understandings.title: Investigating limiting factors experimentally
understandings.summary: Use methods to vary CO2 concentration, light intensity or temperature; propose and test hypotheses about limiting factors and identify independent and dependent variables.

understandings.title: CO2 enrichment experiments and future growth
understandings.summary: Use enclosed greenhouse studies and free-air CO2 enrichment (FACE) experiments to predict future photosynthesis and plant growth; identify controlled variables and weigh lab versus field control.

understandings.title: Photosystems as pigment arrays
understandings.summary: Photosystems are membrane-bound arrays of chlorophyll and accessory pigments, found in cyanobacteria and chloroplasts, with a special reaction-centre chlorophyll that emits an excited electron.

understandings.title: Why pigments work as organised arrays
understandings.summary: Explain the advantages of grouping many pigment types into a photosystem, recognising that one isolated pigment molecule could not carry out any part of photosynthesis.

understandings.title: Photolysis of water in photosystem II
understandings.summary: Photosystem II splits water; its protons and electrons are used in photosynthesis while oxygen is waste. Appreciate the huge biological and geological impact of oxygen production on Earth.

understandings.title: Chemiosmosis makes ATP in thylakoids
understandings.summary: Electron carriers pump protons to build a gradient that drives ATP synthase; electrons come from photosystem I in cyclic or photosystem II in non-cyclic photophosphorylation.

understandings.title: Photosystem I reduces NADP
understandings.summary: NADP is reduced by gaining two electrons from photosystem I and a hydrogen ion from the stroma; use paired terms consistently (NADP/reduced NADP or NADP+/NADPH).

understandings.title: Thylakoid as light-dependent reaction site
understandings.summary: Locate where in the thylakoid photolysis, chemiosmotic ATP synthesis and NADP reduction take place.

understandings.title: Carbon fixation by Rubisco
understandings.summary: Rubisco fixes CO2 onto RuBP to give glycerate 3-phosphate. It is Earth's most abundant enzyme and is needed in high amounts in the stroma because it is slow and weak at low CO2.

understandings.title: Making triose phosphate
understandings.summary: Glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) is converted to triose phosphate (TP) using ATP and reduced NADP.

understandings.title: RuBP regeneration keeps the Calvin cycle going
understandings.summary: Using ATP, five triose phosphates are rearranged into three RuBP; if glucose is the product, five-sixths of TP must be recycled. Individual reaction details are not needed.

understandings.title: Building other compounds from Calvin cycle products
understandings.summary: All carbon in a photosynthesiser is fixed in the Calvin cycle; carbohydrates, amino acids and other compounds are made, with mineral nutrients, from cycle intermediates. No pathway details required.

understandings.title: Light-dependent and light-independent reactions depend on each other
understandings.summary: Explain why darkness halts the light-dependent reactions and why a shortage of CO2 stops photosystem II working.

required_skills: write a word equation for photosynthesis
calculate Rf values and identify pigments from a chromatogram
read absorption spectra labelled with wavelengths and colours
calculate photosynthesis rates from O2/CO2 data and plot an action spectrum
design experiments on limiting factors, stating hypotheses and identifying independent, dependent and controlled variables

visualisation.reason: Light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle are processes; limiting factors are relationships

topics.title: Chemical signalling
big_questions: How can a cell pick out one chemical message among the many it is exposed to?
What happens inside a cell between a signal arriving and the cell responding?

understandings.title: Receptors bind specific signalling chemicals
understandings.summary: Receptors are proteins with binding sites specific to particular signalling chemicals; use the term ligand for the signal.

understandings.title: Quorum sensing in bacteria
understandings.summary: Bacteria use chemical signals to sense population density and act together; use bioluminescence in the marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri as the example.

understandings.title: Functional categories of animal signals
understandings.summary: Distinguish hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and calcium ions as different functional categories of signalling chemical in animals.

understandings.title: Chemical variety of hormones and neurotransmitters
understandings.summary: Hormones may be amines, proteins or steroids; neurotransmitters include amino acids, peptides, amines and nitric oxide. Suggest why so many different chemicals serve as signals.

understandings.title: Local versus long-distance signalling
understandings.summary: Contrast blood-borne hormones acting at a distance with neurotransmitters diffusing across a synaptic gap to act locally.

understandings.title: Membrane receptors versus intracellular receptors
understandings.summary: Compare transmembrane and cytoplasmic/nuclear receptors, including the placement of hydrophilic and hydrophobic amino acids and whether the ligand enters the cell or stays outside.

understandings.title: Receptors trigger signal transduction
understandings.summary: Ligand binding to a receptor starts a chain of responses inside the cell, known as a signal transduction pathway.

understandings.title: Neurotransmitter receptors alter membrane potential
understandings.summary: Using the acetylcholine receptor: binding opens an ion channel in the receptor, positive ions diffuse in, and the resulting voltage change across the membrane can trigger further effects.
