understandings.title: G protein-coupled receptors
understandings.summary: Explain how G protein-coupled receptors pass a signal into the cell, and appreciate that humans have a very large number of them.

understandings.title: How epinephrine (adrenaline) receptors work
understandings.summary: Outline epinephrine signalling via a G protein and cyclic AMP as second messenger; note that both names persist worldwide as an example of scientific naming conventions.

understandings.title: Tyrosine kinase receptors and insulin
understandings.summary: Insulin binds a membrane receptor, causing tyrosine phosphorylation inside the cell and a cascade ending with vesicles carrying glucose transporters moving to the membrane. No further detail needed.

understandings.title: Intracellular receptors and gene expression
understandings.summary: Steroid hormones (oestradiol, progesterone, testosterone) bind and activate receptors inside the cell; the activated receptor binds specific DNA sequences to promote transcription.

understandings.title: Oestradiol and progesterone on target cells
understandings.summary: Limit to oestradiol acting on hypothalamus cells that secrete GnRH, and progesterone acting on endometrium cells.

understandings.title: Positive and negative feedback in signalling
understandings.summary: Distinguish positive from negative feedback regulation of signalling pathways and briefly outline one example of each.

visualisation.reason: Signal-transduction pathways are step-by-step processes

topics.title: Neural signalling
big_questions: How does a neuron create and send an electrical signal using only ions?
How does one neuron pass its message to the next cell?

understandings.title: Neurons carry electrical impulses
understandings.summary: A neuron has a cell body (nucleus and cytoplasm) with long fibres: a single long axon and several shorter dendrites, along which impulses are conducted.

understandings.title: Sodium–potassium pumping sets resting potential
understandings.summary: ATP-driven pumping moves Na+ and K+ in opposite directions, building gradients; explain membrane polarisation, membrane potential and why the resting potential is negative.

understandings.title: Nerve impulses as travelling action potentials
understandings.summary: A nerve impulse is an action potential propagated along a fibre; it is electrical because positively charged ions move.

understandings.title: Why impulse speeds differ
understandings.summary: Compare speeds in squid giant axons versus thin unmyelinated fibres, and myelinated versus unmyelinated fibres; describe correlations and use correlation coefficients and R² to judge their strength.

understandings.title: Synapses as junctions between cells
understandings.summary: Synapses link neurons to neurons or to effector cells; consider chemical synapses only, and understand that signals cross them in one direction.

understandings.title: Neurotransmitter release at the presynaptic membrane
understandings.summary: Depolarisation of the presynaptic membrane causes calcium ions to enter, and calcium acts as an internal signal triggering neurotransmitter release.

understandings.title: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials
understandings.summary: Neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds transmembrane receptors, generating an excitatory potential; use acetylcholine, which acts at many synapses including neuromuscular junctions.

understandings.title: Depolarisation and repolarisation in action potentials
understandings.summary: Explain the roles of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, and why the threshold potential must be reached before sodium channels open.

understandings.title: Local currents propagate action potentials
understandings.summary: Explain how sodium ions diffusing along the inside and outside of the axon bring the next region to threshold, so the impulse moves along the fibre.

understandings.title: Reading oscilloscope traces of nerve activity
understandings.summary: Interpret oscilloscope traces of resting and action potentials in terms of events at the membrane, and measure impulse frequency (impulses per second).

understandings.title: Saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres
understandings.summary: Pumps and channels are concentrated at nodes of Ranvier, so the action potential jumps from node to node, making conduction faster.

understandings.title: External chemicals that disrupt synapses
understandings.summary: Use neonicotinoid pesticides as an example of blocking synaptic transmission, and cocaine as an example of blocking neurotransmitter reuptake.

understandings.title: Inhibitory neurotransmitters and hyperpolarisation
understandings.summary: Inhibitory neurotransmitters produce inhibitory postsynaptic potentials by hyperpolarising the postsynaptic membrane.

understandings.title: Summation of excitatory and inhibitory inputs
understandings.summary: Inputs from many presynaptic neurons combine in the postsynaptic neuron, and their net effect decides, all-or-nothing, whether it depolarises to fire.

understandings.title: Pain detection by free nerve endings
understandings.summary: Free nerve endings in the skin contain channels that open in response to heat, acid or chemicals such as capsaicin; the inflow of positive ions can trigger impulses that the brain interprets as pain.

understandings.title: Consciousness as an emergent property
understandings.summary: Consciousness arises from interactions among many individual neurons in the brain, an example of an emergent property.

required_skills: describe positive and negative correlations and apply correlation coefficients
use the coefficient of determination (R²) to evaluate how much variation is explained
interpret oscilloscope traces of resting and action potentials
measure impulse frequency from a trace

visualisation.reason: Neuron and synapse are 3D; the action potential happens over time

topics.title: Integration of body systems
big_questions: How do nerves and hormones work together so the body acts as one coordinated whole?
How do feedback loops keep vital variables like heart and breathing rate in check?

understandings.title: Why systems need integration
understandings.summary: Living systems need integration: their parts must be coordinated to achieve an overall function together.

understandings.title: Hierarchy of cells, tissues, organs, systems
understandings.summary: Cells, tissues, organs and body systems form nested subsystems; their integration produces emergent properties, e.g. a cheetah's body systems combine to make it an effective predator.

understandings.title: Organs linked by signals and transport
understandings.summary: Distinguish how nervous and endocrine systems send messages, and use examples to stress the blood system's role in moving materials and energy between organs.

understandings.title: The brain integrates information
understandings.summary: The brain combines and processes information from many inputs and underlies learning and memory; detail such as slow-acting neurotransmitters is not required.

understandings.title: Spinal cord handles unconscious processes
understandings.summary: The spinal cord coordinates processes that happen without conscious thought; be able to tell conscious and unconscious processes apart.

understandings.title: Sensory neurons carry input to the CNS
understandings.summary: Sensory neurons carry messages from receptor cells into the spinal cord and cerebral hemispheres.

understandings.title: Motor neurons carry output to muscles
understandings.summary: Motor neurons carry signals from the cerebral hemispheres to muscles, stimulating them to contract.

understandings.title: Structure of a nerve
understandings.summary: A nerve is a bundle of sensory and motor fibres; use a transverse section to show its protective sheath and both myelinated and unmyelinated fibres.

understandings.title: The pain reflex arc
understandings.summary: Describe an involuntary pain reflex from a free nerve ending in the hand, through one interneuron in the spinal cord's grey matter, to a skeletal muscle effector.

understandings.title: Cerebellum coordinates movement and balance
understandings.summary: Give a general account of how the cerebellum coordinates skeletal muscle contraction and balance in overall body movement.

understandings.title: Melatonin and the sleep–wake cycle
understandings.summary: The pineal gland secretes melatonin in a daily (diurnal) pattern that helps set the circadian cycle of sleeping and waking.

understandings.title: Epinephrine prepares for vigorous activity
understandings.summary: The adrenal glands release epinephrine (adrenaline), whose widespread effects on the body support intense muscle contraction.

understandings.title: Hypothalamus and pituitary control hormones
understandings.summary: Give a general account of how the hypothalamus and pituitary control the endocrine system; anterior versus posterior pituitary differences are not needed.

understandings.title: Feedback control of heart rate
understandings.summary: Baroreceptors (blood pressure) and chemoreceptors (pH, O2, CO2) send input to the medulla, which signals the heart to adjust rate and stroke volume. Include receptor locations.

understandings.title: Feedback control of ventilation rate
understandings.summary: Explain what causes blood pH to change; brainstem chemoreceptors detect this and signals to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles adjust ventilation rate.

understandings.title: Nervous control of peristalsis
understandings.summary: Swallowing and egestion are voluntary, controlled by the CNS; peristalsis in between is involuntary, coordinated by the enteric nervous system (ENS).

understandings.title: Observing tropisms in seedlings
understandings.summary: Record seedling tropisms qualitatively with diagrams and quantitatively by measuring curvature angle; distinguish qualitative from quantitative data and consider precision, accuracy and reliability.

understandings.title: Positive phototropism in shoots
understandings.summary: Shoots grow towards light coming from one side, a directional growth response; other specific tropisms are not required.

understandings.title: Phytohormones as plant signals
understandings.summary: Plants use a variety of chemicals as phytohormones to control growth, development and responses to stimuli.

understandings.title: Auxin efflux carriers create gradients
understandings.summary: Auxin diffuses into plant cells but can only leave through efflux carriers. If neighbouring cells place these carriers on matching sides, auxin is moved from cell to cell and builds up in one region.

understandings.title: Auxin promotes cell elongation
understandings.summary: Auxin causes H+ secretion into the apoplast, acidifying and loosening cellulose cross-links so cells elongate; auxin gradients produce the uneven growth behind phototropism.

understandings.title: Auxin–cytokinin interplay in roots and shoots
understandings.summary: Root tips make cytokinin that travels to shoots, shoot tips make auxin that travels to roots; their interaction keeps root and shoot growth coordinated.

understandings.title: Ethylene and positive feedback in ripening
understandings.summary: Ethylene (ethene) triggers ripening and ripening boosts ethylene output; explain how this positive feedback makes ripening fast and synchronised.

named_examples: pain reflex arc in the hand
required_skills: interpret a transverse section of a nerve
record tropic responses of seedlings using diagrams
measure the angle of curvature of seedlings
distinguish qualitative and quantitative data and assess precision, accuracy and reliability

visualisation.reason: Reflex arcs, feedback loops and phototropism animate well in 2D

topics.title: Defence against disease
big_questions: How does the body tell invaders apart from its own cells and destroy them?
Why do some infections spread through populations while others die out?

understandings.title: Pathogens cause infectious disease
understandings.summary: Many organisms can infect humans; pathogens are usually viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists, and no archaea are known to cause human disease. Note how observation of childbed fever (Vienna) and cholera (London) advanced disease control.

understandings.title: Skin and mucous membranes as first barrier
understandings.summary: The skin and mucous membranes are the first line of defence; skin blocks pathogens both physically and chemically. Diagrams of skin are not needed.

understandings.title: Blood clotting seals cuts
understandings.summary: Platelets release clotting factors, starting a cascade in which thrombin rapidly turns fibrinogen into fibrin, which traps red blood cells to form a clot. No further detail needed.

understandings.title: Innate versus adaptive immunity
understandings.summary: The innate system responds to broad pathogen groups and stays the same through life; the adaptive system responds specifically and builds memory so responses improve. Phagocytes are the only innate component needed.

understandings.title: Phagocytes control infection
understandings.summary: Phagocytes squeeze out of capillaries by amoeboid movement to reach infection sites, recognise pathogens, take them in by endocytosis and break them down with enzymes from lysosomes.

understandings.title: Lymphocytes cooperate to make antibodies
understandings.summary: Lymphocytes circulate in blood and reside in lymph nodes; a person has huge numbers of B-lymphocytes, each producing one specific type of antibody.

understandings.title: Antigens trigger antibody production
understandings.summary: Antigens are usually glycoproteins or proteins on pathogen surfaces; antigens on red blood cells can trigger antibody production after transfusion into someone of a different blood group.

understandings.title: Helper T-cells activate B-cells
understandings.summary: B-cells and helper T-cells are antigen-specific; a B-cell is activated only by binding its antigen and contacting a helper T-cell activated by the same antigen, after which it makes antibodies and memory cells.

understandings.title: Clonal expansion into plasma cells
understandings.summary: Few B-cells match a given antigen, so activated ones divide by mitosis into large clones of plasma cells all secreting the same antibody.

understandings.title: Memory cells give immunity
understandings.summary: Immunity is the ability to clear a specific infection, due to long-lived memory lymphocytes able to make the needed antibodies.

understandings.title: How HIV is transmitted
understandings.summary: HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) spreads in body fluids; give examples of its transmission routes.

understandings.title: HIV infects lymphocytes, leading to AIDS
understandings.summary: HIV kills only certain lymphocyte types, but losing them weakens antibody production and the ability to fight opportunistic infections, resulting in AIDS.

understandings.title: Antibiotics target bacterial processes
understandings.summary: Antibiotics block processes found in bacteria but not eukaryotic cells; explain why they cannot treat viral infections.

understandings.title: Evolution of multiple antibiotic resistance
understandings.summary: Pathogenic bacteria evolve resistance to several antibiotics, so careful use is needed to slow multiresistant strains; new techniques like screening chemical libraries are finding new antibiotics.

understandings.title: Zoonoses jump from animals to humans
understandings.summary: Show how common zoonoses are and how they spread using tuberculosis, rabies and Japanese encephalitis, plus COVID-19 as a recent transfer with major consequences.

understandings.title: Vaccines and immunisation
understandings.summary: A vaccine supplies antigens (or DNA/RNA that codes for them) so the body builds immunity to a particular pathogen without the person developing the disease.

understandings.title: Herd immunity prevents epidemics
understandings.summary: When enough people are immune, transmission is greatly impeded, so individuals depend on each other; consider how vaccine research and its media reporting are evaluated.

understandings.title: Analysing COVID-19 pandemic data
understandings.summary: Evaluate data from the COVID-19 pandemic, calculating both percentage difference and percentage change.

required_skills: calculate percentage difference and percentage change from COVID-19 data

visualisation.reason: The immune response is a multi-step process over time

topics.title: Populations and communities
big_questions: What keeps a population from growing forever?
How do different species in a community depend on, compete with and limit each other?

understandings.title: What counts as a population
understandings.summary: A population is a group of the same species living and normally interbreeding in an area; reproductive isolation separates one population from another.

understandings.title: Estimating population size by random sampling
understandings.summary: Explain why populations are estimated rather than fully counted, why sampling must be random, and that sampling error is the gap between the estimate and the true size.

understandings.title: Quadrat sampling for sessile organisms
understandings.summary: Use random quadrats to estimate numbers of countable sessile plants or animals; use a calculator to find the standard deviation of the mean per quadrat and interpret it as spread (formula not required).

understandings.title: Capture–mark–recapture and the Lincoln index
understandings.summary: Estimate motile populations with the Lincoln index: population = M × N ÷ R (M first marked, N total recaptured, R marked recaptured); know the method's assumptions.

understandings.title: Carrying capacity and resource competition
understandings.summary: Give a simple definition of carrying capacity, with examples of resources whose limited supply sets it.

understandings.title: Density-dependent negative feedback
understandings.summary: Density-independent factors cause fluctuations, while density-dependent factors (competition, predation risk, spread of pathogens and pests) push populations back towards carrying capacity.

understandings.title: Population growth curves
understandings.summary: Study a real ecosystem case study; explain early exponential growth (no lag phase expected) and test against the exponential model by plotting population on a log scale against linear time.

understandings.title: Modelling sigmoid growth
understandings.summary: Collect population growth data to model a sigmoid curve, ideally using yeast or duckweed or another organism that multiplies readily in experiments.

understandings.title: Competition and cooperation within a species
understandings.summary: Explain why members of one species compete, and give a range of real examples of both intraspecific competition and cooperation.

understandings.title: Communities of interacting organisms
understandings.summary: A community is all the interacting populations in an ecosystem, including plants, animals, fungi and bacteria.

understandings.title: Types of interspecific relationship
understandings.summary: Know herbivory, predation, interspecific competition, mutualism, parasitism and pathogenicity, with at least one example of each.

understandings.title: Mutualism benefits both partners
understandings.summary: Explain the benefits to both species in root nodules of legumes (Fabaceae), mycorrhizae of orchids (Orchidaceae), and zooxanthellae in hard corals.

understandings.title: Invasive versus endemic species competition
understandings.summary: Use one local example to show how an introduced species becomes invasive by outcompeting endemic species for resources.

understandings.title: Testing for interspecific competition
understandings.summary: One species doing better without another suggests, but does not prove, competition; compare lab experiments, random-sampling field observations and removal experiments, and distinguish experiments from observations.

understandings.title: Chi-squared test for species association
understandings.summary: Apply a chi-squared test to presence/absence data for two species across sampling sites to assess association, which may suggest interspecific competition.

understandings.title: Predator–prey density-dependent control
understandings.summary: Use a real case study to show predator–prey interactions as density-dependent control of animal populations.

understandings.title: Top-down and bottom-up control
understandings.summary: Communities can be regulated from the top (predators) or bottom (resources); both occur, though one usually dominates in a given community.

understandings.title: Allelopathy and antibiotic secretion
understandings.summary: Both involve releasing chemicals into the environment to deter competitors; give one specific example of each, preferably local.

required_skills: interpret standard deviation of mean quadrat counts (calculated on a calculator)
calculate population size with the Lincoln index
plot population growth on a logarithmic vertical axis to test exponential growth
collect data to model sigmoid population growth
apply a chi-squared test to species presence/absence data

visualisation.reason: Population growth and sampling are best learned by simulation

topics.title: Transfers of energy and matter
big_questions: Why do atoms cycle round an ecosystem while energy passes through and is lost?
Why are there so few top predators compared with plants?

understandings.title: Ecosystems are open systems
understandings.summary: Ecosystems are open: both energy and matter enter and leave. Contrast with closed systems, where only energy crosses the boundary.

understandings.title: Sunlight powers most ecosystems
understandings.summary: Sunlight is the main energy source for most ecosystems, with exceptions such as caves and the deep ocean beyond light; consider what makes a scientific law or generalisation useful.

understandings.title: Chemical energy flows along food chains
understandings.summary: Chemical energy passes to a consumer when it eats the organism at the previous stage of a food chain.

understandings.title: Building food chains and webs
understandings.summary: Construct food chains and webs, ideally for a local community, with arrows pointing in the direction energy and biomass move.

understandings.title: Decomposers feed on dead organic matter
understandings.summary: Decomposers get energy from carbon compounds in faeces, dead parts of organisms and whole dead organisms.

understandings.title: Autotrophs make their own carbon compounds
understandings.summary: Autotrophs use an external energy source to build carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances; energy is needed both for carbon fixation and for building macromolecules.

understandings.title: Photoautotrophs versus chemoautotrophs
understandings.summary: Photoautotrophs use light energy while chemoautotrophs use energy released by oxidation reactions; use iron-oxidising bacteria as the chemoautotroph example.

understandings.title: Heterotrophs rely on other organisms' carbon
understandings.summary: Heterotrophs digest complex carbon compounds (e.g. proteins, nucleic acids) externally or internally, then assimilate the products to build the compounds they need.

understandings.title: Both trophic types respire
understandings.summary: Autotrophs and heterotrophs alike release energy by oxidising carbon compounds in cell respiration; photoheterotrophs are not required.

understandings.title: Assigning trophic levels
understandings.summary: Use the terms producer, primary, secondary and tertiary consumer, recognising that organisms with varied diets can occupy different levels in different chains.

understandings.title: Drawing energy pyramids
understandings.summary: Build energy pyramids from real data for particular ecosystems, showing how much energy passes to each trophic level and how much is lost.

understandings.title: Energy shrinks at each trophic level
understandings.summary: Explain the causes of large energy losses between levels; decomposers and detritivores are usually outside food chains but still matter for energy transformations.

understandings.title: Respiration loses heat to the environment
understandings.summary: Energy transfers are inefficient, so heat is released both when respiration makes ATP and when cells use ATP, in autotrophs and heterotrophs alike.

understandings.title: Energy loss limits food chain length
understandings.summary: Higher levels have fewer or smaller organisms and less biomass, though energy per unit mass stays the same; this restricts how many trophic levels exist.

understandings.title: Primary production by autotrophs
understandings.summary: Primary production is biomass accumulated by autotrophs, measured as mass of carbon per area per time (usually g m⁻² yr⁻¹); biomes differ in how much they accumulate.

understandings.title: Secondary production by heterotrophs
understandings.summary: Secondary production is biomass built up by heterotrophs; it is lower than primary production because carbon is lost as CO2 and water in respiration.

understandings.title: Drawing the carbon cycle
understandings.summary: Draw a carbon cycle diagram showing carbon recycled through photosynthesis, feeding and respiration.

understandings.title: Carbon sinks and carbon sources
understandings.summary: An ecosystem is a net CO2 sink when photosynthesis exceeds respiration and a net source when respiration exceeds photosynthesis.

understandings.title: Combustion releases stored carbon
understandings.summary: Burning biomass, peat, coal, oil and natural gas releases CO2; these stores formed at different times, and although lightning fires occur naturally, humans have greatly raised combustion rates.

understandings.title: Interpreting the Keeling Curve
understandings.summary: Explain both the annual zig-zag and the long-term upward trend of the Keeling curve using photosynthesis, respiration and the burning of fuels.

understandings.title: Respiration and photosynthesis depend on each other
understandings.summary: Aerobic respiration relies on oxygen from photosynthesis and photosynthesis on CO2 from respiration; the huge annual fluxes make this a major autotroph–heterotroph interaction.

understandings.title: All elements are recycled
understandings.summary: Every element organisms use, not just carbon, is recycled in ecosystems, with decomposers playing a central role; details of the nitrogen and other nutrient cycles are not required.

named_examples: peat, coal, oil and natural gas
required_skills: construct food chains and food webs with arrows showing energy flow
construct energy pyramids from ecosystem research data
use units of g m⁻² yr⁻¹ for production
draw carbon cycle diagrams
analyse annual fluctuation and long-term trend in the Keeling Curve

visualisation.reason: Energy pyramids and the carbon cycle are quantitative relationships

topics.title: DNA replication
big_questions: How does a cell make a faithful copy of its entire genome?
How have scientists turned the copying of DNA into tools for medicine and forensics?

understandings.title: Replication makes identical DNA copies
understandings.summary: Replication produces DNA molecules with the same base sequence as the original. Know why this matters: it is needed for reproduction, and for growth and replacing tissues in multicellular organisms.

understandings.title: Semi-conservative copying and base pairing
understandings.summary: Each new double helix keeps one old strand and gains one new strand, built by complementary base pairing. Explain how these two features make copying highly accurate.

understandings.title: Helicase and DNA polymerase roles
understandings.summary: Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between strands; DNA polymerase builds the new strands. Only this general level of detail is needed.

understandings.title: PCR and gel electrophoresis techniques
understandings.summary: PCR copies DNA many times using primers, cycles of temperature change and heat-stable Taq polymerase. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments; explain what the separation is based on.

understandings.title: Uses of PCR and gels
understandings.summary: Be aware of the wide range of uses of these techniques, especially DNA profiling for paternity cases and forensic work. Using more markers lowers the chance of a false match.

understandings.title: DNA polymerase works in one direction
understandings.summary: Distinguish the 5' and 3' ends of a nucleotide strand. DNA polymerases only extend a strand by attaching the 5' end of an incoming nucleotide to the 3' end of the growing strand.

understandings.title: Leading versus lagging strand synthesis
understandings.summary: The leading strand is made continuously from a single RNA primer; the lagging strand is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, each needing its own primer. Use the terms continuous, discontinuous and Okazaki fragments.

understandings.title: Primase, polymerases I and III, ligase
understandings.summary: State the job of DNA primase, DNA polymerase III, DNA polymerase I and DNA ligase during replication, using the prokaryotic system only.

understandings.title: Proofreading by DNA polymerase III
understandings.summary: DNA polymerase III checks its work: if the nucleotide just added at the 3' end is mismatched, it is removed and replaced with the correct one. No other repair mechanisms are required.

required_skills: Interpret gel electrophoresis results from DNA profiles, e.g. matching paternity or forensic samples

visualisation.reason: The replication fork works over time; PCR and gels are step processes

topics.title: Protein synthesis
big_questions: How is a message written in DNA bases turned into a working chain of amino acids?
What keeps protein production accurate, and what happens when it goes wrong?

understandings.title: Transcription builds RNA from DNA
understandings.summary: Transcription makes an RNA copy of a gene using one DNA strand as a template. Know the roles of RNA polymerase in the process.

understandings.title: Base pairing during transcription
understandings.summary: Explain how hydrogen bonds and complementary base pairing set the RNA sequence, including that adenine on the DNA template pairs with uracil in RNA.

understandings.title: DNA templates stay unchanged
understandings.summary: A DNA strand can be transcribed repeatedly without its base sequence being altered. In non-dividing body cells this sequence must stay intact for the cell's whole life.

understandings.title: Transcription switches genes on or off
understandings.summary: Only some genes are expressed at any one time. As the first stage of gene expression, transcription is a key control point for turning genes on and off.

understandings.title: Translation builds polypeptides from mRNA
understandings.summary: Translation uses the base sequence of an mRNA molecule to assemble a polypeptide with a matching sequence of amino acids.

understandings.title: mRNA, ribosomes and tRNA in translation
understandings.summary: Describe the roles of the three components. mRNA attaches to the ribosome's small subunit, and the large subunit can hold two tRNAs at the same time.

understandings.title: Codon–anticodon pairing
understandings.summary: tRNA anticodons pair with complementary mRNA codons to bring the correct amino acid. Use the terms codon and anticodon.

understandings.title: Key features of the genetic code
understandings.summary: Explain why codons must be three bases long, and use the terms degeneracy (several codons per amino acid) and universality (the same code in almost all organisms).

understandings.title: Reading an mRNA codon table
understandings.summary: Use a table of mRNA codons to work out the amino acid sequence encoded by a given mRNA strand.

understandings.title: Ribosome movement and peptide bond formation
understandings.summary: During elongation the ribosome moves along mRNA one codon at a time, joining each new amino acid to the growing chain by a peptide bond. Initiation and termination are not the focus here.

understandings.title: Mutations that alter protein structure
understandings.summary: Know that a change in base sequence can change a protein's structure, and be able to describe one example of a point mutation with this effect (e.g. sickle cell anaemia).

understandings.title: 5' to 3' direction of synthesis
understandings.summary: Explain what it means that both transcription and translation proceed in the 5' to 3' direction.

understandings.title: Transcription starts at the promoter
understandings.summary: Transcription begins at a promoter, where proteins such as transcription factors bind. Specific transcription factors do not need to be named.

understandings.title: DNA that does not code for polypeptides
understandings.summary: Much DNA does not code for polypeptides. Examples needed: sequences that regulate gene expression, introns, telomeres, and genes for rRNA and tRNA in eukaryotes.

understandings.title: Processing eukaryotic mRNA after transcription
understandings.summary: In eukaryotes, introns are cut out and exons joined to make mature mRNA, and a 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added to stabilise it.

understandings.title: Alternative splicing gives protein variants
understandings.summary: Joining different combinations of exons lets one gene code for more than one polypeptide. Only the principle is needed, with no specific examples.

understandings.title: How translation begins
understandings.summary: Describe the small subunit binding at the mRNA's 5' end and moving to the start codon, initiator tRNA and a second tRNA arriving, then the large subunit joining. Know the roles of the A, P and E sites during elongation.

understandings.title: Modifying polypeptides into working proteins
understandings.summary: Many polypeptides need modification before they work. The required example is the two-step conversion of pre-proinsulin into insulin.

understandings.title: Proteasomes recycle amino acids
understandings.summary: A healthy proteome depends on continuous protein breakdown by proteasomes alongside new synthesis, so amino acids are recycled.

named_examples: Point mutation affecting protein structure (e.g. sickle cell anaemia)
A, P and E sites of the ribosome
required_skills: Use an mRNA codon table to deduce the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide

visualisation.reason: Transcription and translation are processes over time

topics.title: Mutation and gene editing
big_questions: What causes the base sequence of a gene to change, and is the change ever directed?
Why can a single change in DNA be harmless, harmful or the raw material of evolution?

understandings.title: Gene mutations as molecular changes
understandings.summary: A gene mutation is a change to the base sequence of a gene. Distinguish substitutions, insertions and deletions.

understandings.title: Effects of base substitutions
understandings.summary: Substitutions create single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Because the code is degenerate, a substitution may or may not change one amino acid in the polypeptide.

understandings.title: Effects of insertions and deletions
understandings.summary: Insertions and deletions often stop a polypeptide working, either by shifting the reading frame or by adding or removing large sections. No specific examples are required.

understandings.title: What causes gene mutations
understandings.summary: Mutations arise from mutagens and from mistakes in DNA replication or repair. Give examples of chemical mutagens and of mutagenic radiation.

understandings.title: Mutations happen at random
understandings.summary: Mutations can occur anywhere in a genome, though some bases mutate more readily. No natural mechanism is known that deliberately changes a particular base to alter a trait.

understandings.title: Germ-line versus somatic mutations
understandings.summary: Mutations in germ cells can be passed to offspring, while mutations in somatic cells are not inherited but can lead to cancer.

understandings.title: Mutation as the origin of variation
understandings.summary: Mutation is the ultimate source of all genetic variation. Most mutations are neutral or harmful to an individual, yet over time they are essential for evolution by natural selection.

understandings.title: Knocking out genes to study function
understandings.summary: Gene knockout disables a gene so its function can be inferred from the effect. Technical details are not required; know that libraries of knockout organisms exist for some model research species.

understandings.title: Gene editing with CRISPR-Cas9
understandings.summary: Explain how CRISPR sequences and the Cas9 enzyme are used to edit genes, and know one example of a successful application. Its natural role in prokaryotes is not required; consider ethical and regulatory issues.

understandings.title: Why some gene sequences are conserved
understandings.summary: Some sequences stay the same or similar across species or over long evolutionary time. Consider two hypotheses: functional constraints on the gene product, and slower mutation rates.

visualisation.reason: A sequence editor shows each mutation's effect; CRISPR animates well

topics.title: Cell and nuclear division
big_questions: How does one cell become many identical cells for growth and repair?
How does nuclear division produce gametes that are all genetically different?

understandings.title: Cell division produces new cells
understandings.summary: New cells in all organisms come from a parent (mother) cell dividing to form two daughter cells.

understandings.title: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm
understandings.summary: Compare how cytoplasm is split: in animal cells a contracting ring of actin and myosin pinches the membrane inwards; in plant cells vesicles build new membrane and cell wall between the daughter cells.

understandings.title: Equal and unequal cytoplasm division
understandings.summary: Cytokinesis is usually but not always equal, and each daughter cell needs at least one mitochondrion and other self-replicating organelles. Use human oogenesis and yeast budding as unequal examples.

understandings.title: Why eukaryotes need mitosis and meiosis
understandings.summary: The nucleus must divide before the cell does, so no cell lacks a nucleus. Mitosis keeps chromosome number and genome unchanged; meiosis halves chromosome number and creates genetic diversity.

understandings.title: DNA replicates before division
understandings.summary: Both mitosis and meiosis follow DNA replication, after which each chromosome is two chromatids held together until anaphase.

understandings.title: Chromosome condensation and movement
understandings.summary: In both divisions chromosomes condense by supercoiling around histones and are moved by microtubules and microtubule motor proteins.

understandings.title: The stages of mitosis
understandings.summary: Name the phases of mitosis and explain how the whole process gives two genetically identical daughter nuclei.

understandings.title: Recognising mitosis phases
understandings.summary: Identify each phase of mitosis from diagrams and from cells seen under a microscope or in micrographs.

understandings.title: Meiosis halves chromosome number
understandings.summary: Use the terms diploid and haploid, outline the two rounds of segregation, and explain how one diploid nucleus gives four haploid nuclei. Explain why meiosis is needed in a sexual life cycle.

understandings.title: Non-disjunction and Down syndrome
understandings.summary: Use Down syndrome as the example of a meiosis error, where chromosomes fail to separate correctly (non-disjunction).

understandings.title: How meiosis creates variation
understandings.summary: Explain how random orientation of bivalents and crossing over produce genetically diverse gametes.

understandings.title: Proliferation for growth, replacement and repair
understandings.summary: Cells proliferate for growth, routine replacement and healing. Examples: plant meristems and early animal embryos for growth; skin for routine replacement and wound healing (skin structure not needed).

understandings.title: Stages of the cell cycle
understandings.summary: Proliferation uses the cell cycle: interphase (G1, S, G2) followed by mitosis and then cytokinesis. Know the order of events.

understandings.title: Growth during interphase
understandings.summary: Interphase is a busy metabolic period in which the cell makes proteins, DNA and other components. Mitochondria and chloroplasts grow and divide to increase in number.

understandings.title: Cyclins control the cell cycle
understandings.summary: Different cyclins rise and fall during the cycle, and a specific cyclin must reach a threshold for the cell to pass each checkpoint. The roles of individual cyclins are not needed.

understandings.title: Mutations in cell-cycle control genes
understandings.summary: Mutations that turn proto-oncogenes into oncogenes, or that disable tumour suppressor genes, can cause uncontrolled cell division.

understandings.title: Comparing benign and malignant tumours
understandings.summary: Tumours differ in division rate, growth and ability to invade and spread. Use benign, malignant, primary and secondary tumour, distinguish cancerous from non-cancerous tumours, and determine mitotic index from cell populations.

required_skills: Identify phases of mitosis in diagrams, microscope slides and micrographs
Determine the mitotic index of a cell population from observations

visualisation.reason: Mitosis and meiosis are processes over time

topics.title: Gene expression
big_questions: How can cells with identical DNA end up doing completely different jobs?
Can the environment leave marks on genes that are passed to the next generation?

understandings.title: Gene expression links genes to phenotype
understandings.summary: Gene expression is how information in a gene affects phenotype, most commonly through transcription, translation and the action of the protein made, such as an enzyme.

understandings.title: DNA-binding proteins regulate transcription
understandings.summary: Transcription is controlled by proteins that bind particular DNA sequences. Include the roles of promoters, enhancers and transcription factors.

understandings.title: mRNA breakdown controls translation
understandings.summary: How long mRNA survives before nucleases destroy it regulates how much protein is made; in human cells this ranges from minutes to days.

understandings.title: Epigenesis and cell differentiation
understandings.summary: Epigenesis is the development of differentiation patterns in a multicellular organism's cells. Epigenetic changes alter phenotype but not genotype, because the base sequence is unchanged.

understandings.title: Genome, transcriptome and proteome compared
understandings.summary: Distinguish a cell's full set of genes, the genes it is transcribing, and the proteins it contains. No cell expresses every gene, and its expression pattern determines how it differentiates.

understandings.title: DNA and histone methylation as tags
understandings.summary: Methylated cytosine in a promoter represses transcription of the gene downstream. Methylated amino acids on histones can either repress or activate transcription; the mechanism is not required.

understandings.title: Inheriting gene expression patterns
understandings.summary: Phenotypic changes can pass to daughter cells or offspring without DNA sequence changes if epigenetic tags such as methylation or histone modification survive mitosis or meiosis.

understandings.title: Environment changes gene expression
understandings.summary: The environment can alter gene expression in cells and organisms. The required example is changes to DNA methyl tags caused by air pollution.

understandings.title: Incomplete erasure of tags in gametes
understandings.summary: Most, but not all, epigenetic tags are removed in eggs and sperm. Illustrate the consequences by explaining the epigenetic basis of differences between tigons and ligers.

understandings.title: Studies of identical twins
understandings.summary: Studies of monozygotic twins are used to investigate how the environment affects gene expression; limit to this purpose.

understandings.title: External signals alter expression patterns
understandings.summary: Know one hormone that changes gene expression and one biochemical example in bacteria, such as lactose or tryptophan regulating their genes.

named_examples: Lactose or tryptophan regulation in bacteria

visualisation.reason: Chromatin and methylation changes are clearer as toggles

topics.title: Water potential
big_questions: What decides whether water moves into a cell or out of it?
Why can a plant cell survive in pure water when a red blood cell bursts?

understandings.title: Water as a solvent
understandings.summary: Explain solvation: solutes form hydrogen bonds with water, and both positive and negative ions are attracted to polar water molecules.

understandings.title: Water moves toward higher solute concentration
understandings.summary: Explain water movement by comparing solute concentrations (never 'water concentration'), using the terms hypertonic, hypotonic and isotonic.

understandings.title: Osmosis into and out of cells
understandings.summary: Predict the net direction of water movement for a cell in a hypotonic or hypertonic environment. In an isotonic environment water still moves, but in dynamic equilibrium.

understandings.title: Plant tissue in different solutions
understandings.summary: Measure changes in length and mass of plant tissue in a range of solutions and deduce the isotonic concentration. Use standard deviation and standard error (formulae not memorised), shown as error bars.

understandings.title: Cells without walls and osmosis
understandings.summary: Cells without walls swell and burst in hypotonic media and shrink and crenate in hypertonic media. Freshwater protists use contractile vacuoles; multicellular animals keep tissue fluid isotonic.

understandings.title: Walled cells: turgor and plasmolysis
understandings.summary: Cells with walls become turgid in hypotonic media as pressure builds against the wall, and plasmolyse in hypertonic media.

understandings.title: Isotonic solutions in medicine
understandings.summary: Explain why isotonic solutions are used, with intravenous fluids and bathing donor organs before transplantation as examples.

understandings.title: Defining water potential
understandings.summary: Water potential is the potential energy of water per unit volume. Absolute values cannot be measured, so values are given relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure and 20°C, usually in kPa.

understandings.title: Water flows down water potential gradients
understandings.summary: Water moves from higher to lower water potential; explain this in terms of potential energy.

understandings.title: Solute and pressure potential combined
understandings.summary: Use ψw = ψs + ψp for walled cells. Solute potential is zero or negative; pressure potential is usually positive in cells but negative in xylem under tension.

understandings.title: Water potential in bathed plant tissue
understandings.summary: Use solute and pressure potentials to explain the changes seen when plant tissue is placed in hypotonic or hypertonic solutions.

named_examples: Contractile vacuoles in freshwater unicellular organisms
Red blood cell crenation and bursting
required_skills: Measure length and mass changes in plant tissue and deduce the isotonic solute concentration
Calculate and use standard deviation and standard error, and plot error bars
Calculate water potential using ψw = ψs + ψp (AHL)

visualisation.reason: Water potential is a relationship between solute and pressure potential

topics.title: Reproduction
big_questions: When is copying yourself a better strategy than mixing genes with a partner?
How do hormones coordinate the body changes needed to produce and nurture offspring?

understandings.title: Sexual versus asexual reproduction
understandings.summary: Compare the two: asexual reproduction gives identical offspring suited to an unchanging environment; sexual reproduction gives new gene combinations, providing variation for adapting to change.

understandings.title: Meiosis and fertilization in life cycles
understandings.summary: Meiosis breaks up the parents' allele combinations and fertilization (fusion of gametes) creates new ones.

understandings.title: How male and female sexes differ
understandings.summary: The defining difference between the sexes is that male gametes travel to female gametes, so they are small with few food reserves; link this to the numbers of gametes made and to reproductive strategies.

understandings.title: Human reproductive system anatomy
understandings.summary: Draw diagrams of the male-typical and female-typical reproductive systems, labelling structures and annotating their functions.

understandings.title: Hormones of the menstrual cycle
understandings.summary: Describe changes in the ovarian and uterine cycles and how oestradiol, progesterone, LH and FSH regulate them through both positive and negative feedback.

understandings.title: Events of human fertilization
understandings.summary: Sperm and egg membranes fuse; the sperm nucleus enters but its tail and mitochondria are destroyed. Both nuclear membranes break down and all chromosomes join a single mitosis giving two diploid nuclei.

understandings.title: Hormones used in IVF
understandings.summary: In IVF the body's normal hormone secretion is first suppressed, then artificial hormone doses cause superovulation.

understandings.title: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
understandings.summary: Outline gamete production in ovules and pollen, pollination, pollen development and fertilization to form an embryo. Plant reproduction is sexual even in hermaphrodite species.

understandings.title: Structure of an insect-pollinated flower
understandings.summary: Draw an insect-pollinated flower, labelling its structures and annotating their functions.

understandings.title: Ways plants promote cross-pollination
understandings.summary: Include pollen and stigma maturing at different times, separate male and female flowers or plants, and transfer of pollen between plants by animals or wind.

understandings.title: Self-incompatibility increases variation
understandings.summary: Self-pollination causes inbreeding, lowering genetic diversity and vigour. Many species have genetic mechanisms ensuring fertilization only happens between gametes from different plants.

understandings.title: Seed dispersal and germination
understandings.summary: Distinguish seed dispersal from pollination, and describe germination as the embryo growing and developing while its stored food is mobilised.

understandings.title: Hormonal control of puberty
understandings.summary: Rising GnRH release from the hypothalamus in childhood triggers increased LH and FSH secretion, which raises sex hormone production and causes the changes of puberty. Limit to this sequence.

understandings.title: Producing sperm and eggs
understandings.summary: Compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis through mitosis, growth, two meiotic divisions and differentiation. Explain why they yield very different numbers of gametes with different amounts of cytoplasm.

understandings.title: Preventing more than one sperm entering
understandings.summary: The acrosome reaction lets a sperm get through the zona pellucida; the cortical reaction then blocks other sperm.

understandings.title: Blastocyst formation and implantation
understandings.summary: Describe how the embryo develops into a blastocyst and implants in the endometrium. Other embryo stages need not be named.

understandings.title: Pregnancy tests detect hCG
understandings.summary: The embryo and early placenta secrete hCG; pregnancy tests use monoclonal antibodies that bind to it.

understandings.title: The placenta supports the foetus
understandings.summary: Know which substances cross the placenta and why the large surface area of its villi matters; the placenta allows the foetus to develop much further inside the uterus than in non-placental mammals.

understandings.title: Hormones in pregnancy and birth
understandings.summary: Progesterone, first from the corpus luteum then the placenta, maintains pregnancy. At birth progesterone falls, allowing oxytocin secretion to rise through positive feedback.

understandings.title: HRT and heart disease risk
understandings.summary: Use HRT as a case study of correlation versus causation: early studies linked HRT to less heart disease, but trials showed slightly higher risk; higher socioeconomic status was the real cause.

named_examples: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and monoclonal antibodies
Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and coronary heart disease
required_skills: Draw and annotate diagrams of the human male-typical and female-typical reproductive systems
Draw and annotate a diagram of an insect-pollinated flower
Distinguish correlation from causation using the HRT epidemiology case (AHL)

visualisation.reason: The menstrual-cycle hormone timeline and anatomy suit 2D interactives

topics.title: Inheritance
big_questions: Why do offspring resemble their parents, yet never exactly?
How do the movements of chromosomes explain the ratios we see in genetic crosses?

understandings.title: Gametes and zygotes in inheritance
understandings.summary: Haploid gametes from each parent fuse to form a diploid zygote, a pattern shared by all sexually reproducing eukaryotes. A diploid cell carries two copies of each autosomal gene.

understandings.title: Carrying out crosses in plants
understandings.summary: Use P, F1, F2 and Punnett grid. Pollination is needed to cross plants; species such as peas can self-fertilise. Crosses are used to breed new crop and ornamental varieties.

understandings.title: Genotype: the alleles an organism carries
understandings.summary: Genotype is the pair of alleles inherited. Use homozygous and heterozygous correctly and distinguish genes from alleles.

understandings.title: Phenotype from genes and environment
understandings.summary: Phenotype is the set of observable traits. Suggest human traits caused only by genotype, only by environment, and by their interaction.

understandings.title: Dominant and recessive alleles
understandings.summary: Explain why a homozygous dominant and a heterozygous individual show the same phenotype.

understandings.title: Phenotypic plasticity
understandings.summary: Organisms can develop traits suited to their environment by changing gene expression, without changing genotype; such changes may be reversible during life.

understandings.title: Phenylketonuria: a recessive disease
understandings.summary: PKU is an autosomal recessive condition caused by a mutated gene for the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine.

understandings.title: SNPs and multiple alleles
understandings.summary: A species' gene pool can contain many alleles of one gene (often differing by single-nucleotide polymorphisms), but a diploid individual carries just two.

understandings.title: ABO blood groups
understandings.summary: ABO blood groups illustrate multiple alleles; write the alleles as IA, IB and i.

understandings.title: Codominance and incomplete dominance
understandings.summary: Codominant heterozygotes show both phenotypes (AB blood group, IAIB); incompletely dominant heterozygotes are intermediate (four o'clock flower, Mirabilis jalapa). Compare at the phenotype level.

understandings.title: Sex chromosomes and sex-linked genes
understandings.summary: The sex chromosome in the sperm decides whether the zygote develops male-typical or female-typical features. The X chromosome carries far more genes than the Y.

understandings.title: Haemophilia as sex-linked disorder
understandings.summary: Use haemophilia as the example of sex-linked inheritance, writing alleles as superscripts on a capital X.

understandings.title: Using pedigree charts
understandings.summary: Deduce inheritance patterns and individual genotypes from pedigree charts. Explain the genetic reasons many societies ban marriage between close relatives, and distinguish inductive from deductive reasoning.

understandings.title: Continuous variation and polygenic traits
understandings.summary: Continuous variation results from many genes and/or the environment, with human skin colour as the example. Distinguish continuous from discrete variables (e.g. ABO group) and calculate mean, median and mode.

understandings.title: Box-and-whisker plots
understandings.summary: Draw box-and-whisker plots for continuous data such as height, showing minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum and outliers. Outliers lie more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles.

understandings.title: Segregation and independent assortment
understandings.summary: Link how chromosomes move in meiosis to the results of dihybrid crosses with two unlinked genes.

understandings.title: Dihybrid Punnett grids
understandings.summary: Use Punnett grids to predict genotype and phenotype ratios for two unlinked autosomal genes, explaining where 9:3:3:1 and 1:1:1:1 come from and when Mendel's second law fails.

understandings.title: Gene loci and their products
understandings.summary: Search databases for human genes and their polypeptides, finding gene pairs on different chromosomes and pairs close together on the same chromosome.

understandings.title: Linkage of autosomal genes
understandings.summary: Explain why alleles of linked genes may not assort independently. Show linked alleles beside vertical lines representing homologous chromosomes.

understandings.title: Identifying recombinants
understandings.summary: Work out the outcome of a test cross (double heterozygote × double recessive) for linked or unlinked genes, and identify recombinants among gametes, offspring genotypes and offspring phenotypes.

understandings.title: Chi-squared test for dihybrid data
understandings.summary: Apply a chi-squared test to dihybrid cross results, using null and alternative hypotheses, observed versus expected values, and significance at p = 0.05. The F2 generation acts as a sample of the population.

named_examples: Four o'clock flower, Mirabilis jalapa (incomplete dominance)
Gene databases for human gene loci
required_skills: Construct Punnett grids for monohybrid and (AHL) dihybrid crosses
Analyse pedigree charts to deduce inheritance patterns and genotypes
Calculate mean, median and mode
Draw box-and-whisker plots and identify outliers using 1.5 × IQR
Search gene databases for loci of human genes (AHL)
Perform a chi-squared test on dihybrid cross data (AHL)

visualisation.reason: Punnett, pedigree and chi-squared tools suit 2D interactives

topics.title: Homeostasis
big_questions: How does the body keep its internal conditions steady when the outside world keeps changing?
What goes wrong, and why does it matter, when a control system fails?

understandings.title: Keeping the internal environment steady
understandings.summary: Homeostasis keeps internal variables within set limits despite external change. Human examples to know: body temperature, blood pH, blood glucose and blood osmotic concentration.

understandings.title: Negative feedback in homeostasis
understandings.summary: Explain why homeostasis relies on negative rather than positive feedback, and how negative feedback returns a variable to its set point whether it has risen above or fallen below it.

understandings.title: Hormonal control of blood glucose
understandings.summary: Describe how pancreatic endocrine cells control insulin and glucagon release, how the hormones travel in blood, and their effects on target cells.

understandings.title: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
understandings.summary: Explain the physiological changes behind each type of diabetes, plus their risk factors, prevention and treatment.

understandings.title: Thermoregulation as negative feedback
understandings.summary: Include peripheral thermoreceptors, the hypothalamus, the pituitary gland and thyroxin, and examples of muscle and adipose tissue acting as effectors.

understandings.title: Human temperature control mechanisms
understandings.summary: Birds and mammals use physiological and behavioural means, but details are for humans only: vasodilation, vasoconstriction, shivering, sweating, uncoupled respiration in brown fat and hair erection.

understandings.title: Kidney roles: osmoregulation and excretion
understandings.summary: Distinguish excretion from osmoregulation (control of osmotic concentration, measured in osmol L⁻¹), and describe the kidney's role in both.

understandings.title: Glomerulus, Bowman's capsule and PCT
understandings.summary: Ultrafiltration in the glomerulus forces small solutes out of the blood into the Bowman's capsule; the proximal convoluted tubule then reclaims useful substances, leaving wastes in the filtrate to form urine.

understandings.title: Function of the loop of Henle
understandings.summary: Active transport of sodium ions out of the ascending limb keeps the medulla's osmotic concentration high, which helps water be reabsorbed from the collecting ducts. Limit to this.

understandings.title: ADH and water reabsorption
understandings.summary: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors adjust ADH release from the pituitary; ADH moves aquaporins between intracellular vesicles and the membranes of collecting-duct cells, changing water reabsorption.

understandings.title: Blood flow shifts with activity
understandings.summary: Compare blood supply to skeletal muscle, gut, brain and kidneys during sleep, wakeful rest and vigorous exercise.

named_examples: Nephron: glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, collecting duct
required_skills: Interpret data on blood flow to organs during sleep, rest and exercise (AHL)

visualisation.reason: The nephron is 3D (AHL); feedback loops suit simulations

topics.title: Natural selection
big_questions: Why do some variants leave more offspring than others, and how does that change a species?
How can we measure evolution happening in a population's genes?

understandings.title: Natural selection drives evolution
understandings.summary: Natural selection acts continuously and, over billions of years, has produced Earth's biodiversity. Darwin's mechanism replacing Lamarckism illustrates a paradigm shift; know the term.

understandings.title: Sources of variation for selection
understandings.summary: Mutation creates new alleles and sexual reproduction creates new combinations of alleles, providing the variation natural selection acts on.

understandings.title: Overproduction and competition
understandings.summary: Organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support, so individuals compete; give examples of resources, such as food, that set the carrying capacity.

understandings.title: Abiotic selection pressures
understandings.summary: Non-living, density-independent factors such as extreme temperatures can act as selection pressures affecting survival; give examples.

understandings.title: Variation in survival and reproduction
understandings.summary: Selection depends on individuals differing in how well adapted they are and how many offspring they leave. Study selection through intraspecific competition, using the concept of fitness.

understandings.title: Only heritable traits evolve
understandings.summary: Evolution requires heritable traits. Characteristics acquired during life from the environment are not encoded in genes, so they are not inherited.

understandings.title: Sexual selection in animals
understandings.summary: Physical and behavioural traits that signal fitness affect mating success and so drive evolution. Use examples such as the plumage of birds of paradise.

understandings.title: Experiments controlling selection pressures
understandings.summary: Interpret data from John Endler's guppy experiments, which modelled natural and sexual selection by manipulating predation pressures.

understandings.title: What a gene pool is
understandings.summary: A gene pool is all the genes, and all their alleles, present in a population.

understandings.title: Allele frequencies in isolated populations
understandings.summary: Use databases to compare allele frequencies in geographically separated populations, including at least one human example.

understandings.title: Selection changes allele frequencies
understandings.summary: Natural selection between individuals with different heritable traits shifts allele frequencies in the gene pool. Combining genetics with Darwin's theory is known as neo-Darwinism.

understandings.title: Directional, disruptive and stabilizing selection
understandings.summary: Distinguish the three patterns of selection and recognise that each one changes allele frequencies.

understandings.title: Hardy–Weinberg equation
understandings.summary: Using p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1, calculate expected genotype frequencies from allele frequencies, or allele frequencies from one known genotype frequency.

understandings.title: Conditions for Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
understandings.summary: Know the conditions for genetic equilibrium. If observed genotype frequencies do not fit the equation, a condition is being broken, such as non-random mating or genotype-dependent survival.

understandings.title: Artificial selection by humans
understandings.summary: Breeders choose individuals with desirable traits in crops and domestic animals. Unintended outcomes such as antibiotic resistance in bacteria result from natural, not artificial, selection.

required_skills: Interpret data from Endler's guppy experiments
Search databases for allele frequencies in isolated populations (AHL)
Calculate allele and genotype frequencies using the Hardy–Weinberg equation (AHL)

visualisation.reason: Natural selection and Hardy–Weinberg are best learned by simulation

topics.title: Stability and change
big_questions: What lets some ecosystems persist almost unchanged for millions of years?
How are human activities pushing ecosystems toward collapse, and can they be restored?

understandings.title: Natural ecosystems can be stable
understandings.summary: Cite evidence that some ecosystems, such as particular forests or deserts, have stayed stable for very long periods—in some cases millions of years.

understandings.title: What ecosystems need to stay stable
understandings.summary: Stability needs an energy supply, nutrient recycling, genetic diversity and climate variables that stay within tolerance limits.

understandings.title: Amazon deforestation as tipping point
understandings.summary: A large rainforest area is needed for transpiration to produce water vapour, cooling, air flows and rainfall; the minimum area is uncertain. Calculate percentage change in forest area.

understandings.title: Mesocosms as ecosystem models
understandings.summary: Set up mesocosms to test variables affecting stability. Sealed glass vessels block matter exchange but allow energy transfer; aquatic or microbial systems work better than terrestrial ones. Care for them following IB experimental guidelines.

understandings.title: Keystone species and stability
understandings.summary: Keystone species have an effect on community structure out of proportion to their abundance, and removing them risks ecosystem collapse.

understandings.title: Sustainable harvesting of wild resources
understandings.summary: Harvesting is sustainable only if slower than replacement. Use one terrestrial plant species and one marine fish species to show how sustainability is assessed.

understandings.title: What makes agriculture sustainable
understandings.summary: Consider soil erosion, nutrient leaching, supply of fertilisers and other inputs, agrochemical pollution and carbon footprint.

understandings.title: Eutrophication from fertiliser leaching
understandings.summary: Explain how nitrate and phosphate leaching from fertilisers causes eutrophication in freshwater and marine ecosystems, including the rise in biochemical oxygen demand (BOD).

understandings.title: Biomagnification of toxins
understandings.summary: Explain how toxins build up to higher concentrations in consumers at higher trophic levels, using DDT and mercury as examples.

understandings.title: Plastic pollution in the oceans
understandings.summary: Plastics persist because they are not biodegradable. Give examples of how micro- and macroplastics harm marine life, and note how media coverage shifted public action.

understandings.title: Rewilding to restore ecosystems
understandings.summary: Rewilding methods include reintroducing apex predators and other keystone species, reconnecting habitats over large areas and reducing human impact. Use Hinewai Reserve, New Zealand, as the example.

understandings.title: Ecological succession and its triggers
understandings.summary: Succession can be started by changes in abiotic conditions and in biotic factors.

understandings.title: Trends during primary succession
understandings.summary: Using a suitable land example, describe increases in plant size, primary production, species diversity, food-web complexity and nutrient cycling.

understandings.title: Cyclical succession
understandings.summary: In some ecosystems communities follow a repeating cycle instead of reaching one fixed climax. Refer to a specific example.

understandings.title: Climax communities and arrested succession
understandings.summary: Given conditions tend to produce a particular climax community, but human activity can stop it forming. Use livestock grazing and wetland drainage as examples.

named_examples: One terrestrial plant and one marine fish species harvested
Livestock grazing and wetland drainage (arrested succession)
required_skills: Calculate percentage change, e.g. in area of forest lost to deforestation
Design and maintain a mesocosm to investigate a variable affecting stability

visualisation.reason: Succession, eutrophication and biomagnification suit timelines and charts

topics.title: Climate change
big_questions: How do human emissions set off warming that can then feed itself?
What happens to species and ecosystems when the timing and places they depend on shift?

understandings.title: Human causes of climate change
understandings.summary: Limit to human-caused rises in atmospheric carbon dioxide and methane concentrations.

understandings.title: Positive feedback in global warming
understandings.summary: Include CO₂ release from the deep ocean, reduced reflection as snow and ice melt, faster decomposition of peat and permafrost organic matter, methane from thawing permafrost, and more droughts and fires.

understandings.title: Boreal forests flipping to carbon sources
understandings.summary: Warmer conditions and less snow bring drought, lower production, browning and more frequent, intense fires in the taiga, burning legacy carbon and turning a carbon sink into a source.

understandings.title: Melting polar ice destroys habitats
understandings.summary: Use emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri), at risk as Antarctic landfast ice breaks out early, and Arctic walruses losing sea ice habitat as examples.

understandings.title: Ocean currents and nutrient upwelling
understandings.summary: Warming of surface waters can prevent upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water, lowering primary production in the ocean and the energy available to marine food chains.

understandings.title: Species ranges shift poleward and upslope
understandings.summary: Use evidence from tropical montane birds moving upslope in New Guinea and North American tree species contracting and spreading northward.

understandings.title: Coral reefs at risk of collapse
understandings.summary: Higher CO₂ acidifies oceans and suppresses coral calcification; higher temperatures cause bleaching. Losing corals can collapse the whole reef ecosystem.

understandings.title: Sequestering carbon in forests and peat
understandings.summary: Evaluate afforestation, forest regeneration and peatland restoration for storing carbon, including the debate over non-native plantations versus native rewilding, and where peat forms.

understandings.title: Phenology: timing of biological events
understandings.summary: Phenology is the study of the timing of biological events such as flowering, budburst, bud set, migration and nesting; day length and temperature act as cues that trigger them.

understandings.title: Climate change breaks phenological synchrony
understandings.summary: If one species uses temperature as its cue and another uses photoperiod, warming can desynchronise them. Examples: Arctic mouse-ear chickweed and migrating reindeer; great tit breeding and caterpillar peaks, or a local example.

understandings.title: More insect generations per year
understandings.summary: Warming lets some insects complete more life cycles in a year, illustrated by the spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus or Dendroctonus micans).

understandings.title: Climate change drives evolution
understandings.summary: Reduced snow cover has changed the relative fitness of grey and brown colour variants of the tawny owl (Strix aluco), an example of evolution caused by climate change.
